1	# Chain discipline
2	
3	**Resident. Not routed.** This file loads with `SKILL.md` and is read by every
4	builder, every reviewer and every orchestrator in this chain, on every job.
5	It is the one document that is about *us* rather than about the page.
6	
7	It exists because of a five-day run (Alunix V3d, 2026-09-15 → 09-20) that spent
8	**37 build rounds on 10 orders**, cost $24 for the last round alone, and ended
9	with the owner's verdict:
10	
11	> *"resten av ändringarna motsvarade inte riktigt heller mina förväntningar även
12	> om de utfördes på papper."*
13	> — Anton, 2026-09-20
14	
15	Nothing in that run failed for lack of craft. Every ordered point was built and
16	rendered. It failed because **the chain lied to itself five times and believed
17	each lie** — and every lie became a build round before anyone caught it. The
18	rules below are those five lies and their fixes, plus the four method changes
19	that came out of the same run.
20	
21	**The rule everything else serves:** *a measurement you have not proven against
22	a known-broken case is not a measurement, it is a guess with a number on it.*
23	
24	---
25	
26	## 1 · Measurement
27	
28	### M1 · Register every custom property before you read it
29	
30	`getPropertyValue('--tx')` on an **unregistered** custom property returns the
31	token stream — `clamp(0,calc((0.3214 - 0.2258) / 0.1613),1)` — not a number.
32	`parseFloat` on that is `NaN`, and `NaN` silently compares as `0` in every filter
33	and every `if`.
34	
35	**What it cost:** the `--slit-p` filter was inert through round 18 *and* through
36	two of Astra's review passes without anyone noticing. It then convinced the lead
37	that a colour draw had not started when `--tx` was in fact `0.59`, and that
38	false reading was written up as a finding before it was caught.
39	
40	**The rule.** Every numeric custom property that any script, probe or reviewer
41	reads must be declared:
42	
43	```css
44	@property --tx     { syntax: '<number>'; inherits: true; initial-value: 0; }
45	@property --slit-p { syntax: '<number>'; inherits: true; initial-value: 0; }
46	```
47	
48	Declare it when the property is created, not when a measurement fails. If you
49	are reading a property that is not declared, **that is the finding** — declare
50	it first, then measure.
51	
52	**The check that proves the check:** run `parseFloat(getComputedStyle(el)
53	.getPropertyValue('--tx'))` against the *current, undeclared* state first. It
54	must return `NaN`. A version of this check that returns a number against both a
55	declared and an undeclared property is measuring nothing.
56	
57	### M2 · Never judge an act in a preview mode
58	
59	A `?preview=<name>` mode is a convenience that lands the page at a scroll
60	position. It is **not** evidence that the act renders correctly at that
61	position, and it drifts silently the moment the act's scroll window changes.
62	
63	**What it cost:** when plan 067 recomputed the act's window from hard-coded
64	numbers to calculated ones, every preview mode kept aiming at the old window. At
65	`tes-till-ritning-3` the sheet sat **1329 px below the viewport**. Every review
66	that had used the preview modes since — Astra's included — had been judging the
67	wrong scroll position.
68	
69	**The rule.** Before you judge an act from a preview mode, prove the mode lands
70	where it claims: read the element's bounding box against the viewport in that
71	mode and assert the overlap you expect. Failing that, **measure in real wheel
72	scroll** — `mouse.wheel`, 20 px steps, both directions — and say in your report
73	which method you used.
74	
75	### M3 · Every geometric check proves itself against a broken variant first
76	
77	Run each structural check **against a deliberately broken build** before you run
78	it against the real one. A check that returns green against both a broken and a
79	correct page measures nothing, and it will do so quietly, forever.
80	
81	**What it cost:** it has happened three times in this project. Astra discarded
82	two of her own probe versions in r21 for exactly this reason, and rebuilt her
83	column probe in r22 after a false negative.
84	
85	**The rule.** Every check ships with its injected fault, named in the report:
86	*"`.chapter-plate{clip-path:none;height:+900px}` → N hits, clean build → 0."*
87	A check reported without its broken-case value is not evidence and may not be
88	cited as one.
89	
90	---
91	
92	## 2 · Verification
93	
94	### V1 · A review surface never caches
95	
96	**What it cost:** `board.py` sent only `Last-Modified`, no cache headers. Chrome
97	applied heuristic freshness and served a previous round without revalidating.
98	The owner reviewed stale code **at least twice**, concluded nothing had been
99	built, and had to ask *"är det ens något gjort?"* — a reasonable conclusion from
100	what he was actually looking at.
101	
102	Fixed in `scripts/board.py` (`Cache-Control: no-store, must-revalidate`). The
103	rule outlives the fix: **any surface a human uses to judge work must be
104	uncacheable, and must say so in a header, not in a hope.**
105	
106	If you are ever handed a review surface and cannot state its cache behaviour,
107	assume it is lying to you until you have force-reloaded it once.
108	
109	### V2 · Verify in the render, not in the bytes
110	
111	**What it cost:** the lead grepped the served cell over HTTP, found the change,
112	and reported *"ändringarna finns"* — while the owner was looking at a page that
113	did not have it. Bytes on a server prove nothing about what a browser paints.
114	
115	**The rule.** "It is in the file" is not a verification. "It is in the response
116	body" is not a verification. The verification is **a rendered image of the page
117	the human will actually open**, read as an image, by the person making the claim.
118	When the two disagree, the render wins, and the discrepancy is itself the finding.
119	
120	---
121	
122	## 3 · Orchestration
123	
124	### O1 · Run Codex directly, never through a wrapper agent
125	
126	`Agent(codex-review)` cost **305,000 Opus tokens per round**. Inside that, the
127	actual Codex call was **one request, 24 images in, 6.3 kB of text out** — billed
128	to the OpenAI quota, not to ours. The other ~300k was an Opus subagent
129	re-doing the measurement work before asking the question.
130	
131	**The rule.** Drive `codex exec` from the shell. `scripts/astra.py` takes a
132	prompt file, a screenshot glob and an output path, and reads the answer back.
133	Screenshots come from a capture script; the prompt comes from you; the verdict
134	costs almost nothing.
135	
136	**What you must NOT drop along with the wrapper.** The wrapper verified every
137	Codex finding against the file and the pixels before releasing it. In r21, three
138	of Codex's four findings fell to that check. **The verification step is
139	mandatory and it is now yours.** A Codex verdict is a draft, never a finding.
140	
141	`astra.py` refuses two failure modes by construction and both matter: an empty
142	response is an **error**, not "no findings"; and more than ~28 images produces
143	sludge, so the selection must be narrowed rather than padded.
144	
145	### O2 · A plan that is not on disk does not exist
146	
147	**What it cost:** an architect subagent reported a complete plan **three times**
148	without being able to save it, and said so only when asked for the files
149	directly. A builder was nearly dispatched against a plan that was never written.
150	
151	**The rule.** `subagent_type: Plan` is read-only. Before any builder is
152	dispatched, **`Read` the plan file from disk and confirm it is the plan you
153	think it is.** A plan reported in a message is a draft. The artifact is the file.
154	
155	Same rule for reference baselines, målbilder and captured screenshots: if the
156	path cannot be opened right now, it is not an input.
157	
158	---
159	
160	## 4 · Review
161	
162	### R1 · Aesthetic review is a sanctioned mode
163	
164	This is the single largest method gain in the run, and it was nearly lost.
165	
166	`agents/codex-review.md` was written for code and measurements. In r23 it was
167	instead given the mandate *"varför är detta fult, och vad skulle göra det
168	vackert"*, with the customer's rejection treated as correct by definition and the
169	reviewer instructed to find **what it had missed**. The result was the best
170	review in the project's history. Astra wrote, in plain terms:
171	
172	> *"Jag mätte att den klippta rektangeln äger 44 % av viewporten och kallade det
173	> 'en hel yta som förändras'. Jag mätte formens area och tog den för närvaro."*
174	
175	...and then produced a direction a builder could draw from, rather than a defect
176	list.
177	
178	**The rule.** When the owner rejects work that passed every gate, the failure is
179	not in the gates — it is that no one was asked the aesthetic question. Dispatch
180	Astra in **`mode: aesthetic`**, with these framings:
181	
182	- The customer has already judged it and the customer is right by definition.
183	  Your job is not to defend the work; it is to find what you failed to see.
184	- Name *why* it is ugly in the terms of form — area, weight, rhythm, contrast,
185	  what owns the viewport — not in adjectives.
186	- Weight the answer in `fidelity` and `ceiling`. An aesthetic pass whose output
187	  is a defect list has failed at its one job.
188	
189	**What this does not license.** An aesthetic pass may not re-choose the palette,
190	the type or the direction — that is still a Step 2 decision and still a
191	gate-order violation. It judges how well the *committed* direction is executed,
192	and where the execution reads as empty. The distinction is exact: **"this is
193	badly executed against its own intent" is a finding; "it would look better as
194	something else" is not.**
195	
196	### R2 · A rule in prose needs a mechanical test
197	
198	**What it cost:** F-018 (*the page never narrates itself*) was written into
199	`FEEDBACK.md`, `anti-patterns.md`, `gates.md`, `copy-gate.md` and
200	`production-tells.md` — and then broken by the very next sentence the chain
201	delivered:
202	
203	> *"Vi har ingen husstil. Formen kommer ur verksamheten, och därför valde vi de
204	> två projekt som ligger längst ifrån varandra."*
205	
206	New words, same posture. The sentence explains **the page's own selection** to
207	the reader; nobody asked why those two examples are on the page. It passed the
208	scanner because the rule was written for microtext and this was set in body size.
209	
210	**The rule.** Every copy rule that names a *shape* rather than a word gets a
211	mechanical check, or it will be broken by the next fluent paragraph. F-018's
212	check is `scripts/self_reference_scan.py`: it flags every sentence whose subject
213	is the page, the section, the example or the selection. Run it on the rendered
214	copy, and run it against the sentence above first — it must flag it.
215	
216	A prose rule with no test is a preference, and preferences lose to fluency.
217	
218	---
219	
220	## 5 · The round ladder
221	
222	The five rules above stop the chain lying. This one stops the spiral.
223	
224	**37 rounds for 10 orders** was not a speed problem. It was that **no round was
225	ever allowed to finish before the next one started.** Round 23 built nine ordered
226	points and never ran its own § Verification; the nine were then judged
227	"executed on paper" and the level not reached, which is the only verdict possible
228	when nobody checked.
229	
230	**The ladder, in order, no skipping:**
231	
232	1. **Plan on disk** (O2). Read it before dispatching.
233	2. **Build one round.**
234	3. **Verify that round completely** — its own plan's § Verification, all of it,
235	   not the parts that fit the remaining budget. Disk space, quota and time are
236	   not verification exemptions; if they run out, the round is **incomplete**, and
237	   that is what gets reported.
238	4. **Only then** does the next round start.
239	
240	**A round may not be retro-fitted.** If round N's verification reveals a fault,
241	the fix is round N+1 — never a silent edit folded into round N+2's build.
242	
243	**And the reporting rule that follows from all of it:** a round whose images
244	nobody has looked at has not been verified, whatever the log says. Do not report
245	a build as done on the strength of a green exit code. The builder reporting
246	"grinden grön" while the lead's own reading found a new fault is not a rare
247	event — it happened in r20 and r22 of this run.
248	
249	---
250	
251	## 6 · Where these rules are enforced
252	
253	| Rule | Written into | Mechanised by |
254	|---|---|---|
255	| M1 register properties | this file | the `@property` block; check returns `NaN` on undeclared |
256	| M2 preview modes | this file | bounding-box assertion, or wheel scroll |
257	| M3 broken-variant first | this file · `design-verify` | every probe ships its injected fault |
258	| V1 no caching | this file | `scripts/board.py` `Cache-Control` |
259	| V2 render not bytes | this file · `agents/design-critic.md` | the review contract's `recapture` disposition |
260	| O1 Codex direct | this file · `agents/codex-review.md` | `scripts/astra.py` |
261	| O2 plan on disk | this file | `Read` the file before dispatch |
262	| R1 aesthetic mode | this file · `agents/codex-review.md` | `mode: aesthetic` in the dispatch |
263	| R2 rule needs a test | this file · `copy-gate.md` | `scripts/self_reference_scan.py` |
264	
265	**The one-line version, if you keep only one:** *the customer's rejection is
266	evidence, the chain's own measurement is a claim, and an unverified round is not
267	finished — it is unfinished, and says so.*
268

# Chain discipline

**Resident. Not routed.** This file loads with `SKILL.md` and is read by every
builder, every reviewer and every orchestrator in this chain, on every job.
It is the one document that is about *us* rather than about the page.

It exists because of a five-day run (Alunix V3d, 2026-09-15 → 09-20) that spent
**37 build rounds on 10 orders**, cost $24 for the last round alone, and ended
with the owner's verdict:

> *"resten av ändringarna motsvarade inte riktigt heller mina förväntningar även
> om de utfördes på papper."*
> — Anton, 2026-09-20

Nothing in that run failed for lack of craft. Every ordered point was built and
rendered. It failed because **the chain lied to itself five times and believed
each lie** — and every lie became a build round before anyone caught it. The
rules below are those five lies and their fixes, plus the four method changes
that came out of the same run.

**The rule everything else serves:** *a measurement you have not proven against
a known-broken case is not a measurement, it is a guess with a number on it.*

---

## 1 · Measurement

### M1 · Register every custom property before you read it

`getPropertyValue('--tx')` on an **unregistered** custom property returns the
token stream — `clamp(0,calc((0.3214 - 0.2258) / 0.1613),1)` — not a number.
`parseFloat` on that is `NaN`, and `NaN` silently compares as `0` in every filter
and every `if`.

**What it cost:** the `--slit-p` filter was inert through round 18 *and* through
two of Astra's review passes without anyone noticing. It then convinced the lead
that a colour draw had not started when `--tx` was in fact `0.59`, and that
false reading was written up as a finding before it was caught.

**The rule.** Every numeric custom property that any script, probe or reviewer
reads must be declared:

```css
@property --tx     { syntax: '<number>'; inherits: true; initial-value: 0; }
@property --slit-p { syntax: '<number>'; inherits: true; initial-value: 0; }
```

Declare it when the property is created, not when a measurement fails. If you
are reading a property that is not declared, **that is the finding** — declare
it first, then measure.

**The check that proves the check:** run `parseFloat(getComputedStyle(el)
.getPropertyValue('--tx'))` against the *current, undeclared* state first. It
must return `NaN`. A version of this check that returns a number against both a
declared and an undeclared property is measuring nothing.

### M2 · Never judge an act in a preview mode

A `?preview=<name>` mode is a convenience that lands the page at a scroll
position. It is **not** evidence that the act renders correctly at that
position, and it drifts silently the moment the act's scroll window changes.

**What it cost:** when plan 067 recomputed the act's window from hard-coded
numbers to calculated ones, every preview mode kept aiming at the old window. At
`tes-till-ritning-3` the sheet sat **1329 px below the viewport**. Every review
that had used the preview modes since — Astra's included — had been judging the
wrong scroll position.

**The rule.** Before you judge an act from a preview mode, prove the mode lands
where it claims: read the element's bounding box against the viewport in that
mode and assert the overlap you expect. Failing that, **measure in real wheel
scroll** — `mouse.wheel`, 20 px steps, both directions — and say in your report
which method you used.

### M3 · Every geometric check proves itself against a broken variant first

Run each structural check **against a deliberately broken build** before you run
it against the real one. A check that returns green against both a broken and a
correct page measures nothing, and it will do so quietly, forever.

**What it cost:** it has happened three times in this project. Astra discarded
two of her own probe versions in r21 for exactly this reason, and rebuilt her
column probe in r22 after a false negative.

**The rule.** Every check ships with its injected fault, named in the report:
*"`.chapter-plate{clip-path:none;height:+900px}` → N hits, clean build → 0."*
A check reported without its broken-case value is not evidence and may not be
cited as one.

---

## 2 · Verification

### V1 · A review surface never caches

**What it cost:** `board.py` sent only `Last-Modified`, no cache headers. Chrome
applied heuristic freshness and served a previous round without revalidating.
The owner reviewed stale code **at least twice**, concluded nothing had been
built, and had to ask *"är det ens något gjort?"* — a reasonable conclusion from
what he was actually looking at.

Fixed in `scripts/board.py` (`Cache-Control: no-store, must-revalidate`). The
rule outlives the fix: **any surface a human uses to judge work must be
uncacheable, and must say so in a header, not in a hope.**

If you are ever handed a review surface and cannot state its cache behaviour,
assume it is lying to you until you have force-reloaded it once.

### V2 · Verify in the render, not in the bytes

**What it cost:** the lead grepped the served cell over HTTP, found the change,
and reported *"ändringarna finns"* — while the owner was looking at a page that
did not have it. Bytes on a server prove nothing about what a browser paints.

**The rule.** "It is in the file" is not a verification. "It is in the response
body" is not a verification. The verification is **a rendered image of the page
the human will actually open**, read as an image, by the person making the claim.
When the two disagree, the render wins, and the discrepancy is itself the finding.

---

## 3 · Orchestration

### O1 · Run Codex directly, never through a wrapper agent

`Agent(codex-review)` cost **305,000 Opus tokens per round**. Inside that, the
actual Codex call was **one request, 24 images in, 6.3 kB of text out** — billed
to the OpenAI quota, not to ours. The other ~300k was an Opus subagent
re-doing the measurement work before asking the question.

**The rule.** Drive `codex exec` from the shell. `scripts/astra.py` takes a
prompt file, a screenshot glob and an output path, and reads the answer back.
Screenshots come from a capture script; the prompt comes from you; the verdict
costs almost nothing.

**What you must NOT drop along with the wrapper.** The wrapper verified every
Codex finding against the file and the pixels before releasing it. In r21, three
of Codex's four findings fell to that check. **The verification step is
mandatory and it is now yours.** A Codex verdict is a draft, never a finding.

`astra.py` refuses two failure modes by construction and both matter: an empty
response is an **error**, not "no findings"; and more than ~28 images produces
sludge, so the selection must be narrowed rather than padded.

### O2 · A plan that is not on disk does not exist

**What it cost:** an architect subagent reported a complete plan **three times**
without being able to save it, and said so only when asked for the files
directly. A builder was nearly dispatched against a plan that was never written.

**The rule.** `subagent_type: Plan` is read-only. Before any builder is
dispatched, **`Read` the plan file from disk and confirm it is the plan you
think it is.** A plan reported in a message is a draft. The artifact is the file.

Same rule for reference baselines, målbilder and captured screenshots: if the
path cannot be opened right now, it is not an input.

---

## 4 · Review

### R1 · Aesthetic review is a sanctioned mode

This is the single largest method gain in the run, and it was nearly lost.

`agents/codex-review.md` was written for code and measurements. In r23 it was
instead given the mandate *"varför är detta fult, och vad skulle göra det
vackert"*, with the customer's rejection treated as correct by definition and the
reviewer instructed to find **what it had missed**. The result was the best
review in the project's history. Astra wrote, in plain terms:

> *"Jag mätte att den klippta rektangeln äger 44 % av viewporten och kallade det
> 'en hel yta som förändras'. Jag mätte formens area och tog den för närvaro."*

...and then produced a direction a builder could draw from, rather than a defect
list.

**The rule.** When the owner rejects work that passed every gate, the failure is
not in the gates — it is that no one was asked the aesthetic question. Dispatch
Astra in **`mode: aesthetic`**, with these framings:

- The customer has already judged it and the customer is right by definition.
  Your job is not to defend the work; it is to find what you failed to see.
- Name *why* it is ugly in the terms of form — area, weight, rhythm, contrast,
  what owns the viewport — not in adjectives.
- Weight the answer in `fidelity` and `ceiling`. An aesthetic pass whose output
  is a defect list has failed at its one job.

**What this does not license.** An aesthetic pass may not re-choose the palette,
the type or the direction — that is still a Step 2 decision and still a
gate-order violation. It judges how well the *committed* direction is executed,
and where the execution reads as empty. The distinction is exact: **"this is
badly executed against its own intent" is a finding; "it would look better as
something else" is not.**

### R2 · A rule in prose needs a mechanical test

**What it cost:** F-018 (*the page never narrates itself*) was written into
`FEEDBACK.md`, `anti-patterns.md`, `gates.md`, `copy-gate.md` and
`production-tells.md` — and then broken by the very next sentence the chain
delivered:

> *"Vi har ingen husstil. Formen kommer ur verksamheten, och därför valde vi de
> två projekt som ligger längst ifrån varandra."*

New words, same posture. The sentence explains **the page's own selection** to
the reader; nobody asked why those two examples are on the page. It passed the
scanner because the rule was written for microtext and this was set in body size.

**The rule.** Every copy rule that names a *shape* rather than a word gets a
mechanical check, or it will be broken by the next fluent paragraph. F-018's
check is `scripts/self_reference_scan.py`: it flags every sentence whose subject
is the page, the section, the example or the selection. Run it on the rendered
copy, and run it against the sentence above first — it must flag it.

A prose rule with no test is a preference, and preferences lose to fluency.

---

## 5 · The round ladder

The five rules above stop the chain lying. This one stops the spiral.

**37 rounds for 10 orders** was not a speed problem. It was that **no round was
ever allowed to finish before the next one started.** Round 23 built nine ordered
points and never ran its own § Verification; the nine were then judged
"executed on paper" and the level not reached, which is the only verdict possible
when nobody checked.

**The ladder, in order, no skipping:**

1. **Plan on disk** (O2). Read it before dispatching.
2. **Build one round.**
3. **Verify that round completely** — its own plan's § Verification, all of it,
   not the parts that fit the remaining budget. Disk space, quota and time are
   not verification exemptions; if they run out, the round is **incomplete**, and
   that is what gets reported.
4. **Only then** does the next round start.

**A round may not be retro-fitted.** If round N's verification reveals a fault,
the fix is round N+1 — never a silent edit folded into round N+2's build.

**And the reporting rule that follows from all of it:** a round whose images
nobody has looked at has not been verified, whatever the log says. Do not report
a build as done on the strength of a green exit code. The builder reporting
"grinden grön" while the lead's own reading found a new fault is not a rare
event — it happened in r20 and r22 of this run.

---

## 6 · Where these rules are enforced

| Rule | Written into | Mechanised by |
|---|---|---|
| M1 register properties | this file | the `@property` block; check returns `NaN` on undeclared |
| M2 preview modes | this file | bounding-box assertion, or wheel scroll |
| M3 broken-variant first | this file · `design-verify` | every probe ships its injected fault |
| V1 no caching | this file | `scripts/board.py` `Cache-Control` |
| V2 render not bytes | this file · `agents/design-critic.md` | the review contract's `recapture` disposition |
| O1 Codex direct | this file · `agents/codex-review.md` | `scripts/astra.py` |
| O2 plan on disk | this file | `Read` the file before dispatch |
| R1 aesthetic mode | this file · `agents/codex-review.md` | `mode: aesthetic` in the dispatch |
| R2 rule needs a test | this file · `copy-gate.md` | `scripts/self_reference_scan.py` |

**The one-line version, if you keep only one:** *the customer's rejection is
evidence, the chain's own measurement is a claim, and an unverified round is not
finished — it is unfinished, and says so.*

# Reference lock

**Load in Step 1b, for every tier.** Refero's research-first method, adapted to this
skill's four-tier gate (`SKILL.md` Step 2): Tier 0 locked · Tier 1 derive · Tier 2
reference · Tier 3 invent. The lock is not a Tier-2-only artifact — every tier states
one before Step 2 runs, because every tier is a claim about where the direction comes
from, and an unstated claim is how Tier 1 gets skipped in favour of invention.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Reads** | The brief, Step 1 pre-flight findings, Step 2 tier evidence (`DESIGN.md`, brand assets, user URL/screenshot, or nothing), the design catalog, 21st.dev for tech/SaaS shots, Refero MCP when configured. |
| **Does** | Runs the research loop below, captures references as read images (never from memory), fills the reference-lock block and decision ledger, checks the build against anti-averaging and token/media-role preservation. |
| **Writes** | Nothing persisted by default — the lock is stated in-session, out loud, before Step 2 and Step 4. When the system is being locked to a portable file, its fields feed [`design-md.md`](design-md.md). |
| **Human checks** | Whether the named primary reference is actually the dominant voice in the build, not a label pasted over an averaged result — the one judgment this file cannot automate. |

---

## What changes per tier

The loop is identical; only what plays the role of "the reference" changes.

- **Tier 0 — locked.** Reconstructed, not invented: read `DESIGN.md` and what's
  already built from it, and write down what "preserve" means. Primary = the
  locked system itself.
- **Tier 1 — derive.** Primary = the brand evidence (logo, wordmark, hex, deployed
  site, `tailwind.config` colours). Borrowed details may come from competitor or
  category references; they extend the language, never re-set it.
- **Tier 2 — reference.** Primary = the user-supplied URL or screenshot. Refero's
  native case; the fields map straight across.
- **Tier 3 — invent.** Primary = the invented world's own bible
  ([`invention.md`](invention.md)) — locking against it stops the second component
  from drifting into a different invented world than the first.

At every tier, a major visual choice with no source in the lock is not shipped.

---

## A brief is not a build target

Refero states the rule this file exists to enforce, in one sentence: *"**A brief is not a
build target.** Before implementation, lock either a user-provided visual source, an
existing product/design-system target, a selected generated mockup, or an explicit
reference-locked direction approved for direct build."*

This is the sentence that closes the skip route. When the direction feels obvious and the
signature act is being built straight from the brief, the visual target still gets named
first — one line saying what this is being built *toward* and what must not drift:

```text
Build target: [existing UI / user screenshot / URL capture / selected mockup / approved reference lock]
What must not drift: [canvas, typography, accent roles, layout, media, density]
```

If no target exists and the visual direction is material, explore options or get one
reference-locked direction approved. A build whose only stated source is the brief is a
build with no source at all.

## Research loop

Six angles, not one query:

1. **Broad aesthetic** — the mood in plain language ("warm coastal Nordic hospitality").
2. **Domain / category** — what this business actually is.
3. **Known brand** — a specific strong player in the segment, named.
4. **Register** — the row from `SKILL.md`'s register table this brief lands in.
5. **Anti-reference** — one thing this build should *not* look like, sharpening the
   boundary the same way a rejected direction does in the lock block below.
6. **Cross-domain wildcard** — one reference from *outside* the category, chosen for a
   quality rather than a subject. *"A banking app can be inspired by a meditation app's
   calm."* Upstream's map:

   | This brief's domain | Look at |
   |---|---|
   | Healthcare | Meditation apps (calm), fitness apps (motivation), journaling (reflection) |
   | Finance | Productivity tools (clarity), weather apps (data viz), news apps (hierarchy) |
   | Education | Games (engagement), music apps (progression), social apps (community) |
   | E-commerce | Editorial sites (storytelling), gallery apps (browsing), travel (discovery) |
   | Enterprise | Consumer apps (polish), design tools (power + clarity), docs (wayfinding) |

   *"Don't force connections — but don't limit yourself to competitors either."* Competitors
   solve the same problem the same way, which is precisely how a category default becomes
   invisible. `select.py --wildcard` is the catalogue-side version of this angle.

**Quality over quantity: *"5 excellent references beat 20 mediocre ones."*** A wall of
screenshots is not research; it is deferred judgment. Curate down before capturing.

Then: **capture 3–4 full references as images and read them**, long pages in
viewport-sized slices. Memory returns wrong facts — two market-leading pages
turned out to *centre* their heroes, and one coloured words inside the headline
instead of switching typeface, opposite of what was assumed before the images
were opened.

**Every captured reference carries two lines, not one:**

```text
What to take: [the specific element or quality to learn from]
What to leave: [what does not apply here]
```

*"This prevents wholesale copying."* A reference with no lesson is decoration, and a
reference with only a "take" line is the one that quietly becomes the whole build. The
"leave" line is also what makes the primary/borrowed split below enforceable rather than
declarative.

**Extract more than colour and type.** From each reference, read out: layout system,
section rhythm and composition · card, button and surface treatments · borders, shadows,
radius · elevation and depth rules · imagery, graphic and illustration treatment · media
asset strategy (real asset, generated, code-native primitive, product screenshot, or
placeholder) · do and don't rules · **one memorable visual move to adapt**. A lock that
carries a palette and a typeface and nothing structural is why a build "referenced" a page
it looks nothing like.

**Give each source a bounded job.** *"Primary style: overall mood, density, and structure.
Secondary styles: specific borrowed details. User context: adapt everything to the product,
audience, and task."* A source with no job is a source that gets averaged.

From the 3–4 captured, pick **one primary** and take **1–2 borrowed details** from
the rest. Nothing else survives into the lock.

**Flag accessibility failures in the references themselves.** *"A beautiful reference with
2:1 contrast ratios is not inspiration — it's a cautionary tale."* Name it when you capture
it, so the trait does not travel into the lock as craft.

### Sources, in order

1. **The design catalog** — `~/anti-slop-design/design-catalogue/`,
   `python scripts/query.py --family … --register … --grammar …`. Query by the
   register named in `SKILL.md`'s table, not by vibe.
2. **User-supplied URL or screenshot** — Tier 2's native input; also valid at any
   tier as a borrowed-detail source.
3. **21st.dev** for tech/SaaS product shots — browse, screenshot, study the
   treatment; borrow the principle and rebuild it in the locked tokens, never paste
   a component with its own palette into a Tier 0–2 build.
4. **Refero MCP**, if configured — `refero_search_styles` → `refero_get_style`.
   Optional. State plainly when it is not configured rather than silently skipping
   it; do not treat its absence as license to skip the research loop itself.

### When the results are weak

Sparse or generic results are a query problem before they are a source problem. Climb this
ladder before concluding the catalogue has nothing (Refero `mcp-tools.md` § If Results Are
Weak):

1. **Broaden the query.**
2. **Remove extra adjectives or constraints.** Two adjectives and a register is usually one
   adjective too many.
3. **Search adjacent categories.**
4. **Try a known-product or best-brand query.** Name a specific strong player instead of
   describing a type.
5. **Inspect later pages.** The first page of any index is the most averaged part of it.

Only after all five is "no usable reference in this register" a finding — and then it is
stated in the lock, not silently converted into invention.

### Transcribe the category's live headlines

Before writing a word of copy, read the **five best live pages in the category and quote
their headlines verbatim** into the lock. *"The bar is what the reader has already seen, not
what sounds nice in isolation"* (`upstream/slopmonster/references/sources.md`). Five lines,
copied exactly, with the source named. They belong here rather than in
[`copy-gate.md`](copy-gate.md) because they are a *reference* capture: the same discipline
as the four screenshots, applied to language, and read before the copy pass rather than
during it.

## The reference-lock block

Verbatim fields, filled before any code:

```text
Primary reference/direction: [one dominant source, named]
Preserve: [3-5 traits that must survive: canvas, type, accent, layout, density, media]
Borrow only: [1-2 specific secondary details]
Role rules: [source token/component meanings to preserve — CTA-only, code-only, decorative-only]
Media strategy: [photo:unsplash | photo:pexels | product surface | drawn system | generated | placeholder]
Reject: [defaults/averages that would collapse the direction]
Token commitments: [canvas, type, accent, radius, border/shadow, imagery — each with its role]
```

**Media strategy is an enum, not prose.** Pick exactly one value per media slot so
drift is visible at a glance: a hero declared `photo:unsplash` that quietly becomes
a CSS gradient is a caught regression; a hero declared "some kind of photo" is not.

## Decision ledger

Every entry in the lock traces back through this table:

| Decision | Source | Source rule/role | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| [palette / type / layout / media choice] | [reference / catalog query / brand asset / craft rule] | [token or component role to preserve] | [reason specific to this brief] |
| **Memorable detail** | [the reference the move was adapted from] | [what the move does on this page] | [why *this* brief earns it] |

**A major visual choice with no row here is not shipped.** Not "shipped and
justified after" — the row exists before the choice does.

**The `Memorable detail` row is mandatory, and the rule applies to it too.** Refero's
requirement is unambiguous: *"Create at least one memorable detail: a visual move,
interaction, layout choice, or copy detail users would remember."* No row, not shipped —
including for the signature act itself, which is the row most often left blank on the
grounds that it is obvious. An example of a filled row from upstream's own worked case:
*"Memorable detail | 'Operational value' strip showing saved hours/cost by plan | Brief +
analytics product context | Metric strip as evidence, not decoration | Makes pricing feel
tied to outcome."*

## The asset lock

Written **before** anyone starts searching or generating — Step 5b has a pipeline but no
spec upstream of it, and an asset sourced without a spec is an asset chosen by whatever the
search returned. One block per media slot:

```text
Asset role: [hero image / texture / illustration / thumbnail / cutout]
Slot: [dimensions / aspect ratio / location on the page]
Art direction: [source, palette, subject, rendering, crop, density]
Avoid: [wrong palette, extra text, brand drift, generic placeholders]
```

The `Avoid` line is the one that earns its keep: it is the reject field applied to a single
asset, and it is what a QA pass compares the delivered frame against.
*"Generated assets must be placed into the implementation before handoff or documented as
blocked"* — never quietly downgraded to a gradient. That downgrade is the media-role drift
this file's next section already bans, caught one step earlier.

---

## Anti-averaging

Choose a dominant direction. Secondary references contribute narrow, named details;
they do not get to soften the primary one. The failure mode is specific: a dark
workbench reference, an acid-yellow document site, and a serif editorial page do not
average into a warm cream canvas with muted clay accents — **dark + acid + serif is
not cream + orange + polite serif.** Dark → cream, saturated → muted clay, sharp →
rounded, distinctive layout → generic hero-and-sections: each swap is the
intersection eating the direction, not synthesis.

Run these against the lock before shipping — ported from `anti-ai-slop.md`:

- **Identity test.** If the first viewport could belong to any other company,
  branding lost to averaging. Add the one detail that makes this unmistakably *this*
  brand's build.
- **Editorial test.** If swapping the logo for a coffee shop, boutique hotel, or
  literary magazine still makes the hero feel plausible, the build has drifted into
  generic calm-editorial slop regardless of what the lock says on paper.
- **Screenshot test.** Would this pass next to real products in the named
  register, or does it read as the safe middle every other page also landed on?

A lock that names a dominant primary and still fails these three was averaged during
implementation, not during research — check the built page against the lock's
"Reject" line specifically.

## Token-role and media-role preservation

**Token-role preservation.** A source's role for a colour, radius, shadow, or
component is part of the token, not separable from it. A CTA-only accent used as a
section background, a code-only syntax colour promoted to UI chrome, or a decorative
gradient turned into a core surface are all role drift. Preserve the role or drop
the token — never repurpose it to make a layout "work."

**Media-role preservation.** An image-led reference never collapses to text-only
because the image was hard to produce. If the real asset genuinely is not
available, the placeholder must be honest, not silent:

```text
Placeholder — [slot name]
Aspect: [ratio, e.g. 16:9 desktop / 4:3 mobile]
Art direction: [subject, lighting, crop the real asset will match]
Alt: [describes the intended real subject, not "placeholder image"]
```

A placeholder with no aspect ratio, no art direction, and generic alt text is the
same failure as no image at all — it just fails one render cycle later.

---

10	| 1 | `scrub` | `data-sc-act="scrub" data-sc-span="2.6" data-sc-dwell="0.35"` on the section; `data-sc-scrub data-sc-src="…"` on the `<video>` | span 2.2–3.0 for a hero | ≤2 per page. The wheel scrubs a pre-rendered clip; spend it on the open |
11	| 2 | `pin` | `data-sc-act="pin" data-sc-span="3"` | span ≥1.2 (below that, progress jumps 0→1 in one notch) | The frame holds, copy states cross over inside it |
12	| 3 | `pan` | `data-sc-act="pan" data-sc-span="3.2"`; rail gets `data-sc-pan="0.08"` | ~1vh per item + 1 | Lateral = breadth, not hierarchy. Overflow must be measured, not assumed |
13	| 4 | `reveal` | `data-sc-reveal="up|down|left|right|iris" data-sc-reveal-at="0.15 0.55"` | — | `clip-path` wipe = change of state. `iris` once per page at most |
14	| 5 | `kinetic` | `data-sc-kinetic="lines|words|chars"` on a cued heading | — | Lines almost always right, chars ~never. One kinetic headline per act |
15	| 6 | `parallax` | `data-sc-parallax="-0.6"` | rate is **hundreds of px total travel**, not a fraction — usable range 0.3–1.5 (framed), 1–2 (full-bleed) | Never on body copy. 3 layers is plenty |
16	| 7 | `count` | `data-sc-count="0 4,200" data-sc-count-at="0.1 0.5"` | 1.2–1.8s outside an act (`data-sc-count-ms`) | Only real numbers. No verified figure, no counter |
17	| 8 | `flow` + `in` | `data-sc-in data-sc-stagger="70"` on the wrap | stagger 30–80ms | The rest of the page. Fires once, opacity+14px rise, ~620ms ease-out |
18	| 9 | pointer: `tilt` / `magnet` / `spotlight` | `data-sc-tilt="7"` (5–9°), `data-sc-magnet="0.28"` (0.2–0.35, CTA only), `data-sc-spotlight` (publishes `--sc-mx`/`--sc-my`) | — | Gated to `(hover:hover) and (pointer:fine)`. Never gated on reduced motion (F-011, superseded 2026-09-07) |
19	
20	`drift` (`data-sc-drift="#0A0806"` on an act) is not a device, it's a
21	property: the page ground interpolates toward it while the act is live. 3–5
22	stops, one theme family. On a page of many *short* acts several can be
23	part-way through at once — paint grounds per section instead of drifting; see
24	upstream §10.
25	
26	## The cue contract — what verification actually catches you on
27	
28	`data-sc-cue="from [to [rampIn [rampOut]]]"`, all in act progress 0–1.
29	
30	| Form | Behaviour |
31	|---|---|
32	| `"0.2"` | fades in at 0.2, **holds to the end of the act** |
33	| `"0.1 0.6"` | in, plateau, out (ramps default 30% of window each) |
34	| `"0 0.78 0"` | **greet**: full opacity at act start, then fades — the hero form |
35	| `"0 1 0 0"` | **greet and hold**: full at p=0, no ramp either end |
36	
37	**The plateau is the point.** Without one, a cue is a triangle that touches full
38	opacity for a single instant, so the reader has to stop on exactly the right
39	pixel to see the line at full strength and every heading reads slightly faded.
40	`"0.1 0.9 0.15 0.4"` — fast in, long slow out — is the confident form. Cue
41	windows on a pinned act **overlap by design**, roughly 15% of the act: the
42	outgoing line is still fading while the next arrives, and a gap between cues
43	reads as a loading failure.
44	
45	Five rules, each one a real bug this fixture has caught:
46	
47	- **A hero cue needs the greet form.** A plain `"0 0.7"` means the first
48	  screen every visitor sees has no headline on it.
49	- **The last act's cue must hold** (one value). A two-value close cue fades
50	  the CTA out before the page ends.
51	- **Only the last act may hold.** A one-value cue on a *middle* pinned act
52	  stays lit through the whole un-pin slide — the line travels a full viewport
53	  up, crosses fixed chrome, overlaps the next section. Invisible until
54	  measured; shows up as a contrast failure nobody meant.
55	- **Ground or greet.** A pinned stage is fully visible ~1vh *before* its own
56	  progress leaves 0. A plain two-value first cue shows an empty stage for
57	  that whole travel — give the act a ground (image/colour already doing
58	  work) or open with a greet cue.
59	- **Clip time ≠ cue time.** A `scrub` clip is mapped across the stage's
60	  *entire visible life* (default), not across the pinned travel, because the
61	  stage is on screen for a viewport before the pin starts and after it ends.
62	  Cues keep using `p` (they belong to the pin); the clip uses a separately
63	  computed `vp`. Reaching for `data-sc-clip-map="travel"` reintroduces the
64	  freeze — there's almost no reason to.
65	
66	Two more that a harness will not catch by itself:
67	
68	- **Pan overflow must be measured, not assumed.** The rail travels exactly
69	  `scrollWidth - viewport`; a rail narrower than the viewport travels **zero**
70	  and the act reads as a still. `rail.scrollWidth - innerWidth` — check it,
71	  don't guess.
72	- **Parallax rate is hundreds of pixels total, not a viewport fraction** — see
73	  the table above. A rate of 0.35 across three viewport-heights of scroll is
74	  35px: invisible.
75	
76	Composing an act: devices stack (a pinned stage can hold a scrub clip, a
77	parallax layer, a kinetic headline, a spotlight at once), but one thing is the
78	reason the act exists — say that thing in one sentence or the act has none.
79	
80	## The playhead is lerped (§1)
81	
82	The mechanism the whole kit's smoothness rests on, and the one F-012 kept
83	being blamed on. **Scroll never writes `currentTime`.** It writes a *target*,
84	and a standalone rAF loop walks the clip toward that target at a fixed
85	fraction per frame:
86	
87	> *"Wheel events do not arrive at a constant rate, so a 1:1 write reproduces
88	> every gap in them and the clip reads as a stutter rather than a glide."*
89	
90	Three mechanisms, all on by default:
91	
92	- **Lerp 0.18 per frame.** `data-sc-lerp` overrides it, on the mount root for
93	  the whole page or on a single `<video>`. **Clamped to 0.02–1 and never read
94	  as 0** — a 0 lerp is a playhead that never moves. Reach for an override only
95	  when a page's clips are short enough that 0.18 visibly lags the hand.
96	  Worldflight wants 0.12 instead; see [`pace.md`](pace.md).
97	- **Deadband: 8 ms desktop, 20 ms mobile.** A write smaller than that costs a
98	  seek and shows nothing; on a phone it costs more than it shows.
99	- **Seek coalescing.** No seek is queued while the decoder is still resolving
100	  the last one. *"A fast flick otherwise piles seeks up and freezes the clip."*
101	
102	An offscreen clip that has already reached its target stops being touched at
103	all. (Upstream states the offscreen skip without a threshold value; the 0.002
104	figure belongs to `shoot.mjs`'s settle test, below, not to this skip.)
105	
106	This applies to **every** scrub clip on the page, act or worldflight. It is
107	also why the shooter waits for the playhead to arrive before each frame:
108	
109	> *"A frame captured mid-lerp is a frame the page never actually holds."*
110	
111	`shoot.mjs` settles on `|current − target| < 0.002 && !seeking`. Any harness
112	the chain runs against a scrubbed page inherits that requirement — a
113	screenshot taken mid-lerp makes the run unrepeatable, not merely imprecise.
114	
115	Upstream also drops the damping to 1.0 (no smoothing at all) under reduced
116	motion. **That branch does not port: F-011.** The lerp is unconditional here,
117	which is the correct behaviour anyway — it is a smoothing mechanism, not an
118	effect, and turning it off is what produces the stepping fault.
119	
120	## Layered scenes: where the premium feel comes from (§6)
121	
122	Ported from `devices.md` § 6, measured off a reference premium site and proven
123	on a live build. A flat page moves as one sheet; a layered page is a stack of
124	cut-out planes sliding past each other, and *"the eye reads that differential
125	motion as depth before it reads anything else."* It is the single biggest
126	difference between a page that feels built and one that feels assembled, and
127	it costs three transparent images and a multiplier each.
128	
129	- **Plan the planes back to front.** Far ridge, mid ridge, the product, then a
130	  **foreground plane in front of the product**. The product sits between mid
131	  and front, so the foreground overtakes it as the reader scrolls. That
132	  overtaking is the move.
133	- **Small rate differences, not big ones.** The reference hero lags the far
134	  plane **31%** behind the page, the mid plane **17%**, the product **20%**,
135	  and foreground and copy travel at exactly **1×**. Adjacent planes differ by
136	  **10–30%**. Larger stops reading as distance and starts reading as things
137	  sliding around. **Copy always rides at 1×.**
138	- **Shape the foreground for the product.** A straight-edged foreground covers
139	  the product's CTA within a few hundred pixels of scroll. Cut it so it dips
140	  where the product is and rises at the edges, and the button stays in view
141	  two to three times as long.
142	- **Every plane is solid below its silhouette.** Cut-out art that fades to
143	  transparent at the bottom lets the plane behind show through as the planes
144	  separate. Fill each column solid from its first opaque pixel down.
145	- **Fade the section floor.** Planes travel past the section's bottom edge and
146	  are clipped there. A gradient to the page ground over the last 200–300 px,
147	  layered above every plane, hides the clip line at any scroll position.
148	
149	Three traps, each of which cost a round of fixes:
150	
151	- A global `img { max-width: 100% }` shrinks an absolutely positioned plane to
152	  the viewport on phones, so the far layer never shows. **Planes carry
153	  `max-width: none` and a fixed pixel width.**
154	- **Never `transition: transform` on a parallaxed element.** A reveal class is
155	  the usual culprit. The transition eases every per-frame scroll write over
156	  its own duration, and on a phone that reads as the product lagging a full
157	  second behind the thumb. Parallaxed elements transition **opacity only**.
158	- Replacing a plane's art under the same filename ships nothing to a phone
159	  holding the old bytes. **New art gets a new name.**
160	
161	`data-sc-parallax` and a raw scroll multiplier are the same tool in different
162	units. What matters is the **ratio between planes**, not the absolute travel.
163	
164	## The premium fade-in, exactly (§8)
165	
166	The `flow` + `in` device is most of the page, so its defaults decide how the
167	page feels between the acts:
168	
169	| Ingredient | Value |
170	|---|---|
171	| Opacity | 0 → 1 |
172	| Rise | **~14 px** |
173	| Duration | **~620 ms**, ease-out |
174	| Stagger | **30–80 ms**, children in reading order |
175	| Trigger | IntersectionObserver, `-12%` bottom root margin, **fires once** |
176	
177	- **A fade with no rise reads as a loading glitch.** A rise **past 24 px reads
178	  as a slide.** 14 px is the band, not a starting point to tune upward.
179	- The `-12%` margin fires the reveal when the reader is looking, not when the
180	  first pixel clears the fold.
181	- `data-sc-in` is what the engine watches. Without it nothing fires and the
182	  stagger children stay hidden.
183	- **Content that re-hides on the way back up is a defect, not an effect.**
184	- *"Larger, slower, or bouncier is never more premium; the restraint is the
185	  signal."*
186	
187	**A flow section directly after a pinned act takes reduced padding.** The
188	pinned stage needs a full viewport to scroll off, and full `--sc-section`
189	padding on top of that delays the flow section's first content by another
190	screen. The harness will not call it dead scroll — correctly, the stage is
191	moving — and the reader still sees a near-empty screen. Cut the block padding
192	there and start the first reveal near `p = 0`.
193	
194	## Rail settle on `pan` (§3)
195	
196	Lateral travel alone reads as a slideshow on rails. **Give the rail's items a
197	staggered settle driven from `--sc-p`** and they read as a drawer being
198	pulled instead.
199	
200	- **Exempt the first item** — a `pan` act needs its opening content already
201	  present.
202	- **Floor the opacity around 0.55**, so a not-yet-settled card reads as
203	  arriving rather than as failing to load.
204	
205	Upstream gates the settle to `prefers-reduced-motion` — **utgår, F-011**.
206	The settle always runs. What *does* survive from
207	the same passage is the reachability requirement, which is not a motion
208	preference at all: a `pan` rail's transform **is** the navigation, so nothing
209	may zero it and park the act on its first screenful. Every item in a rail
210	stays reachable, and that is checked on the sheet, not assumed.
211	
212	Two more, from the same section:
213	
214	- **Card copy is read while cropped.** Items enter and leave through the
215	  viewport edges, so a heading is half-shown for most of its life, and two
216	  half-headings side by side can read as a third word (`TRACE` beside
217	  `EVALUATE` becoming `RE EVALUATE`). Keep card headings to one or two short
218	  words and expect every line to be read partially cut off.
219	- If three items do not reach half a viewport of overflow, **the fix is more
220	  rail, not wider cards**: put the act's heading in as the first item and a
221	  closing note as the last. Both earn their place, and they add the width the
222	  travel needs.
223	
224	## Devices that cannot share an element (§9)
225	
226	**`magnet`, `parallax` and `cue` all write `transform`.** The magnet writes
227	every frame in its own rAF loop, so it silently wins and the cue's entrance
228	rise is discarded — a visible animation lost to a race, with nothing in the
229	console.
230	
231	- On a magnetic CTA, set **`data-sc-rise="0"`** so the cue writes a no-op
232	  instead of losing to the magnet.
233	- A cued element that wants its own continuous transform drives an **inner
234	  wrapper** from `--sc-p` in CSS, rather than stacking a second device on the
235	  same node.
236	
237	All three pointer devices **interpolate toward** the pointer rather than
238	tracking it directly: *"direct tracking reads as artificial because it carries
239	no momentum."* They stay gated to `(hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)` so
240	touch never fires a false hover — that gate is a pointer-capability query, not
241	a motion preference, and it stands.
242	The reduced-motion half of the same sentence does not port (F-011).
243	
244	## Kinetic type: the mask and the re-split (§5)
245	
246	Each unit slides up from **behind a mask**, so it enters from a clean edge
247	rather than simply fading.
248	
249	- **Line masks must reserve room for descenders.** A mask clipped to the line
250	  box shears the tails off g, y, p and j, *"and that is the single most common
251	  way this effect looks broken."*
252	- **Line splitting measures real line boxes, so it re-runs after
253	  `document.fonts.ready`.** Do not call it on text still loading its face. The
254	  same `fonts.ready` handle earns its place twice over: a webfont swapping in
255	  changes the measured height of every copy block, so anything sized against
256	  those blocks (a scrim plate, a rail) is wrong until it re-measures.
257	- Lines are almost always right; words for a short punch line; characters
258	  approximately never, *"because it turns reading into waiting."*
259	- **One kinetic headline per act, at most.**
260	
261	## What makes a `count` land (§7)
262	
263	- **Ease out, hard.** A cubic ease-out, so most of the distance goes by in the
264	  first third and the last digits settle slowly. *"A linear count reads as a
265	  slot machine."*
266	- **1.2–1.8 s.** Under a second and the reader misses that it moved; past two
267	  and they are waiting for a number they have already guessed.
268	- **Fires at half visibility, once**, so the reader is looking at it when it
269	  starts, and it never re-runs on the way back up.
270	- **Pair it with the fade.** A counter inside a `data-sc-in` stack rises in
271	  with its label and starts ticking as it arrives — *"the same numbers static
272	  on the page read as a spreadsheet."*
273	- Write the target exactly as it should render, commas included; the engine
274	  strips them before parsing and applies `tabular-nums` so the layout does not
275	  jitter.
276	
277	**A concept, fictional or pre-launch brand has no verified figures, so it has
278	no counters.** The device suits a SaaS or agency page and will look good in
279	the score table, *"which is exactly the trap: every number you could put in it
280	would be invented."* Decide this before designing an act around a number, not
281	after. Real brand, real stats, or a different device.
282	
283	## Appendix: pattern vocabulary
284	
285	Named patterns from taste-skill § 10, carried here so orchestrator, builder
286	and reviewer name the same thing. It is a **vocabulary, not a menu** — several
287	entries below are banned as directions elsewhere in the chain (glassmorphism,
288	holographic foil, carousels, gooey menus) and appear here only so a critique
289	can say which trope it is refusing.
290	
291	- **Hero** — Asymmetric Split · Editorial Manifesto · Video/Media Mask ·
292	  Kinetic-Type · Curtain-Reveal · Scroll-Pinned.
293	- **Nav** — Dock Magnification · Magnetic Button (`data-sc-magnet`) · Gooey
294	  Menu · Dynamic Island · Contextual Radial · Floating Speed Dial · Mega Menu
295	  Reveal.
296	- **Layout** — Bento Grid · Masonry · Chroma Grid · Split-Screen Scroll ·
297	  Sticky-Stack Sections.
298	- **Cards** — Parallax Tilt Card (`data-sc-tilt`) · Spotlight Border Card
299	  (`data-sc-spotlight`) · Glassmorphism Panel · Holographic Foil ·
300	  Tinder Swipe Stack · Morphing Modal.
301	- **Scroll** — Sticky Scroll Stack · Horizontal Scroll Hijack (= `pan`) ·
302	  Locomotive / Sequence Scroll (= `scrub`) · Zoom Parallax · Scroll Progress
303	  Path · Liquid Swipe Transition.
304	- **Galleries** — Dome Gallery · Coverflow Carousel · Drag-to-Pan Grid ·
305	  Accordion Image Slider · Hover Image Trail · Glitch Effect Image.
306	- **Type** — Kinetic Marquee · **Text Mask Reveal** (massive type as a
307	  transparent window onto video — this is K2's letter-window) · Text Scramble
308	  · Circular Text Path · Gradient Stroke Animation · Kinetic Typography Grid.
309	- **Micro** — Particle Explosion Button · Liquid Pull-to-Refresh · Skeleton
310	  Shimmer · Directional Hover-Aware Button · Ripple Click · Animated SVG Line
311	  Drawing · Mesh Gradient Background · Lens Blur Depth.
312	
313	Names alone are not permission. A pattern still has to clear the fingerprint
314	gate, the register, and `../motion.md` before it ships.
315	
316	## Never restyle the engine's classes (AB06, 2026-09-03)
317	
318	Theme the engine only through its six colour tokens and two fonts. A project rule on
319	`.sc-stage`, `.sc-copy`, `.sc-scrim` or any other `.sc-*` class silently wins over the
320	engine: the console then says `[scrollcraft] act "…" will not pin: its stage computes
321	position:relative` and every pinned act scrolls away, leaving its spacer as dead scroll.
322	Read the console for `[scrollcraft]` warnings before anything else in Step 5, and run
323	`scripts/scroll_verify.py` — a blind one-shot cannot see either. The engine is opt-in per
324	grammar (scrub, pin, pan); a page that keeps the chain's own single set-piece + shared
325	reveal does not need it.

  Worldflight wants 0.12 instead; see [`pace.md`](pace.md).
- **Deadband: 8 ms desktop, 20 ms mobile.** A write smaller than that costs a
  seek and shows nothing; on a phone it costs more than it shows.
- **Seek coalescing.** No seek is queued while the decoder is still resolving
  the last one. *"A fast flick otherwise piles seeks up and freezes the clip."*

An offscreen clip that has already reached its target stops being touched at
all. (Upstream states the offscreen skip without a threshold value; the 0.002
figure belongs to `shoot.mjs`'s settle test, below, not to this skip.)

This applies to **every** scrub clip on the page, act or worldflight. It is
also why the shooter waits for the playhead to arrive before each frame:

> *"A frame captured mid-lerp is a frame the page never actually holds."*

`shoot.mjs` settles on `|current − target| < 0.002 && !seeking`. Any harness
the chain runs against a scrubbed page inherits that requirement — a
screenshot taken mid-lerp makes the run unrepeatable, not merely imprecise.

Upstream also drops the damping to 1.0 (no smoothing at all) under reduced
motion. **That branch does not port: F-011.** The lerp is unconditional here,
which is the correct behaviour anyway — it is a smoothing mechanism, not an
effect, and turning it off is what produces the stepping fault.

## Layered scenes: where the premium feel comes from (§6)

Ported from `devices.md` § 6, measured off a reference premium site and proven
on a live build. A flat page moves as one sheet; a layered page is a stack of
cut-out planes sliding past each other, and *"the eye reads that differential
motion as depth before it reads anything else."* It is the single biggest
difference between a page that feels built and one that feels assembled, and
it costs three transparent images and a multiplier each.

- **Plan the planes back to front.** Far ridge, mid ridge, the product, then a
  **foreground plane in front of the product**. The product sits between mid
  and front, so the foreground overtakes it as the reader scrolls. That
  overtaking is the move.
- **Small rate differences, not big ones.** The reference hero lags the far
  plane **31%** behind the page, the mid plane **17%**, the product **20%**,
  and foreground and copy travel at exactly **1×**. Adjacent planes differ by
  **10–30%**. Larger stops reading as distance and starts reading as things
  sliding around. **Copy always rides at 1×.**
- **Shape the foreground for the product.** A straight-edged foreground covers
  the product's CTA within a few hundred pixels of scroll. Cut it so it dips
  where the product is and rises at the edges, and the button stays in view
  two to three times as long.
- **Every plane is solid below its silhouette.** Cut-out art that fades to
  transparent at the bottom lets the plane behind show through as the planes
  separate. Fill each column solid from its first opaque pixel down.
- **Fade the section floor.** Planes travel past the section's bottom edge and
  are clipped there. A gradient to the page ground over the last 200–300 px,
  layered above every plane, hides the clip line at any scroll position.

Three traps, each of which cost a round of fixes:

- A global `img { max-width: 100% }` shrinks an absolutely positioned plane to
  the viewport on phones, so the far layer never shows. **Planes carry
  `max-width: none` and a fixed pixel width.**
- **Never `transition: transform` on a parallaxed element.** A reveal class is
  the usual culprit. The transition eases every per-frame scroll write over
  its own duration, and on a phone that reads as the product lagging a full
  second behind the thumb. Parallaxed elements transition **opacity only**.
- Replacing a plane's art under the same filename ships nothing to a phone
  holding the old bytes. **New art gets a new name.**

`data-sc-parallax` and a raw scroll multiplier are the same tool in different
units. What matters is the **ratio between planes**, not the absolute travel.

## The premium fade-in, exactly (§8)

The `flow` + `in` device is most of the page, so its defaults decide how the
page feels between the acts:

| Ingredient | Value |
|---|---|
| Opacity | 0 → 1 |
| Rise | **~14 px** |
| Duration | **~620 ms**, ease-out |
| Stagger | **30–80 ms**, children in reading order |
| Trigger | IntersectionObserver, `-12%` bottom root margin, **fires once** |

- **A fade with no rise reads as a loading glitch.** A rise **past 24 px reads
  as a slide.** 14 px is the band, not a starting point to tune upward.
- The `-12%` margin fires the reveal when the reader is looking, not when the
  first pixel clears the fold.
- `data-sc-in` is what the engine watches. Without it nothing fires and the
  stagger children stay hidden.
- **Content that re-hides on the way back up is a defect, not an effect.**
- *"Larger, slower, or bouncier is never more premium; the restraint is the
  signal."*

**A flow section directly after a pinned act takes reduced padding.** The
pinned stage needs a full viewport to scroll off, and full `--sc-section`
padding on top of that delays the flow section's first content by another
screen. The harness will not call it dead scroll — correctly, the stage is
moving — and the reader still sees a near-empty screen. Cut the block padding
there and start the first reveal near `p = 0`.

## Rail settle on `pan` (§3)

Lateral travel alone reads as a slideshow on rails. **Give the rail's items a
staggered settle driven from `--sc-p`** and they read as a drawer being
pulled instead.

- **Exempt the first item** — a `pan` act needs its opening content already
  present.
- **Floor the opacity around 0.55**, so a not-yet-settled card reads as
  arriving rather than as failing to load.

Upstream gates the settle to `prefers-reduced-motion` — **utgår, F-011**.
The settle always runs. What *does* survive from
the same passage is the reachability requirement, which is not a motion
preference at all: a `pan` rail's transform **is** the navigation, so nothing
may zero it and park the act on its first screenful. Every item in a rail
stays reachable, and that is checked on the sheet, not assumed.

Two more, from the same section:

- **Card copy is read while cropped.** Items enter and leave through the
  viewport edges, so a heading is half-shown for most of its life, and two
  half-headings side by side can read as a third word (`TRACE` beside
  `EVALUATE` becoming `RE EVALUATE`). Keep card headings to one or two short
  words and expect every line to be read partially cut off.
- If three items do not reach half a viewport of overflow, **the fix is more
  rail, not wider cards**: put the act's heading in as the first item and a
  closing note as the last. Both earn their place, and they add the width the
  travel needs.

## Devices that cannot share an element (§9)

**`magnet`, `parallax` and `cue` all write `transform`.** The magnet writes
every frame in its own rAF loop, so it silently wins and the cue's entrance
rise is discarded — a visible animation lost to a race, with nothing in the
console.

- On a magnetic CTA, set **`data-sc-rise="0"`** so the cue writes a no-op
  instead of losing to the magnet.
- A cued element that wants its own continuous transform drives an **inner
  wrapper** from `--sc-p` in CSS, rather than stacking a second device on the
  same node.

All three pointer devices **interpolate toward** the pointer rather than
tracking it directly: *"direct tracking reads as artificial because it carries
no momentum."* They stay gated to `(hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)` so
touch never fires a false hover — that gate is a pointer-capability query, not
a motion preference, and it stands.
The reduced-motion half of the same sentence does not port (F-011).

## Kinetic type: the mask and the re-split (§5)

Each unit slides up from **behind a mask**, so it enters from a clean edge
rather than simply fading.

- **Line masks must reserve room for descenders.** A mask clipped to the line
  box shears the tails off g, y, p and j, *"and that is the single most common
  way this effect looks broken."*
- **Line splitting measures real line boxes, so it re-runs after
  `document.fonts.ready`.** Do not call it on text still loading its face. The
  same `fonts.ready` handle earns its place twice over: a webfont swapping in
  changes the measured height of every copy block, so anything sized against
  those blocks (a scrim plate, a rail) is wrong until it re-measures.
- Lines are almost always right; words for a short punch line; characters
  approximately never, *"because it turns reading into waiting."*
- **One kinetic headline per act, at most.**

## What makes a `count` land (§7)

- **Ease out, hard.** A cubic ease-out, so most of the distance goes by in the
  first third and the last digits settle slowly. *"A linear count reads as a
  slot machine."*
- **1.2–1.8 s.** Under a second and the reader misses that it moved; past two
  and they are waiting for a number they have already guessed.
- **Fires at half visibility, once**, so the reader is looking at it when it
  starts, and it never re-runs on the way back up.
- **Pair it with the fade.** A counter inside a `data-sc-in` stack rises in
  with its label and starts ticking as it arrives — *"the same numbers static
  on the page read as a spreadsheet."*
- Write the target exactly as it should render, commas included; the engine
  strips them before parsing and applies `tabular-nums` so the layout does not
  jitter.

**A concept, fictional or pre-launch brand has no verified figures, so it has
no counters.** The device suits a SaaS or agency page and will look good in
the score table, *"which is exactly the trap: every number you could put in it
would be invented."* Decide this before designing an act around a number, not
after. Real brand, real stats, or a different device.

## Appendix: pattern vocabulary

Named patterns from taste-skill § 10, carried here so orchestrator, builder
and reviewer name the same thing. It is a **vocabulary, not a menu** — several
entries below are banned as directions elsewhere in the chain (glassmorphism,
holographic foil, carousels, gooey menus) and appear here only so a critique
can say which trope it is refusing.

- **Hero** — Asymmetric Split · Editorial Manifesto · Video/Media Mask ·
  Kinetic-Type · Curtain-Reveal · Scroll-Pinned.
- **Nav** — Dock Magnification · Magnetic Button (`data-sc-magnet`) · Gooey
  Menu · Dynamic Island · Contextual Radial · Floating Speed Dial · Mega Menu
  Reveal.
- **Layout** — Bento Grid · Masonry · Chroma Grid · Split-Screen Scroll ·
  Sticky-Stack Sections.
- **Cards** — Parallax Tilt Card (`data-sc-tilt`) · Spotlight Border Card
  (`data-sc-spotlight`) · Glassmorphism Panel · Holographic Foil ·
  Tinder Swipe Stack · Morphing Modal.
- **Scroll** — Sticky Scroll Stack · Horizontal Scroll Hijack (= `pan`) ·
  Locomotive / Sequence Scroll (= `scrub`) · Zoom Parallax · Scroll Progress
  Path · Liquid Swipe Transition.
- **Galleries** — Dome Gallery · Coverflow Carousel · Drag-to-Pan Grid ·
  Accordion Image Slider · Hover Image Trail · Glitch Effect Image.
- **Type** — Kinetic Marquee · **Text Mask Reveal** (massive type as a
  transparent window onto video — this is K2's letter-window) · Text Scramble
  · Circular Text Path · Gradient Stroke Animation · Kinetic Typography Grid.
- **Micro** — Particle Explosion Button · Liquid Pull-to-Refresh · Skeleton
  Shimmer · Directional Hover-Aware Button · Ripple Click · Animated SVG Line
  Drawing · Mesh Gradient Background · Lens Blur Depth.

Names alone are not permission. A pattern still has to clear the fingerprint
gate, the register, and `../motion.md` before it ships.

## Never restyle the engine's classes (AB06, 2026-09-03)

Theme the engine only through its six colour tokens and two fonts. A project rule on
`.sc-stage`, `.sc-copy`, `.sc-scrim` or any other `.sc-*` class silently wins over the
engine: the console then says `[scrollcraft] act "…" will not pin: its stage computes
position:relative` and every pinned act scrolls away, leaving its spacer as dead scroll.
Read the console for `[scrollcraft]` warnings before anything else in Step 5, and run
`scripts/scroll_verify.py` — a blind one-shot cannot see either. The engine is opt-in per
grammar (scrub, pin, pan); a page that keeps the chain's own single set-piece + shared
reveal does not need it.

PONYTAIL MODE ACTIVE — level: full

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
3. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
4. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
5. **Can it be one line?** One line.
6. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project. Two rungs work → take the
higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the right one.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications with a `ponytail:` comment (`// ponytail: this exists`), simple reads as intent, not ignorance. Shortcut with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic)? The comment names the ceiling and the upgrade path: `# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`.

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.

Primary Request and Intent: The user issued one long Swedish briefing for **Alunix V3d round 24 (R24)**, a design/build iteration on a single long-scroll landing page (`tests/alunix-r8/runs/V3d/index.html`). Verbatim-critical instructions: - **Read `tests/alunix-r8/runs/V3d/R24-BRIEF.md` first** — *"Den bär rundans nio fel med mätvärden och kontroller, och läget i filen: fel 1, 5 och 9 är redan lagda och ska inte återupprepas. 7	## The feeling curve
8	
9	One line per act in `BRIEF.md`, written **before a single act exists**: the
10	emotion, then what on screen causes it. The emotion is the constraint; the
11	device name only ever appears in the cause column, second.
12	
13	```
14	1  Recognition   their own kitchen counter at 7am, shot at eye height
15	2  Fatigue       the two containers, the mess, held still while copy names it
16	3  Delight       a wipe, and the whole frame is one cold can, condensation running
17	4  Trust         macro texture at a scale the eye cannot get in a shop
18	5  Appetite      the flavours travelling sideways, each one landing whole
19	6  Resolve       everything stops, one can, one line, one place to buy it
20	```
21	
22	Two adjacent acts with the same feeling means one is filler — cut it or
23	change what it does. The curve outranks the Step 1 journey beats: beats say
24	what the visitor learns, the curve says what they feel while learning it, and
25	where they disagree the curve wins.
26	
27	## The peak
28	
29	People remember one peak and the ending; the middle compresses into a general
30	impression. So every build engineers **one** deliberate peak, named in
31	`BRIEF.md` as the sentence a visitor would say to a friend ("the screen went
32	black and then the whole ocean lit up under me" — a moment, not "the hero is
33	impressive"). The peak gets, at the expense of every other act:
34	
35	| It gets | Because |
36	|---|---|
37	| The asset budget | Best generated frames or the only real footage go here |
38	| The silence before it | A quiet act or empty viewport, so the change has something to be a change from |
39	| The most scroll room | Largest `data-sc-span` on the page, `dwell` tuned to settle exactly there |
40	
41	A page with three peaks has none — demote the losers (shorter span, plainer
42	device). The close must resolve, not trail off: the divider collapses, the
43	world lands somewhere, the type quiets — never a fade to an empty stage.

46

48	video" is a device name — no hook. "You drag the letters of the logo apart
