# Feeling curve, peak, signature move, fingerprint gate

Condensed from `upstream/scroll-craft/.../references/feel.md` and
`uniqueness.md` §§3–4. Design the feeling before the acts: a device chosen
before the emotion is a device looking for a reason.

## The feeling curve

One line per act in `BRIEF.md`, written **before a single act exists**: the
emotion, then what on screen causes it. The emotion is the constraint; the
device name only ever appears in the cause column, second.

```
1  Recognition   their own kitchen counter at 7am, shot at eye height
2  Fatigue       the two containers, the mess, held still while copy names it
3  Delight       a wipe, and the whole frame is one cold can, condensation running
4  Trust         macro texture at a scale the eye cannot get in a shop
5  Appetite      the flavours travelling sideways, each one landing whole
6  Resolve       everything stops, one can, one line, one place to buy it
```

Two adjacent acts with the same feeling means one is filler — cut it or
change what it does. The curve outranks the Step 1 journey beats: beats say
what the visitor learns, the curve says what they feel while learning it, and
where they disagree the curve wins.

## The peak

People remember one peak and the ending; the middle compresses into a general
impression. So every build engineers **one** deliberate peak, named in
`BRIEF.md` as the sentence a visitor would say to a friend ("the screen went
black and then the whole ocean lit up under me" — a moment, not "the hero is
impressive"). The peak gets, at the expense of every other act:

| It gets | Because |
|---|---|
| The asset budget | Best generated frames or the only real footage go here |
| The silence before it | A quiet act or empty viewport, so the change has something to be a change from |
| The most scroll room | Largest `data-sc-span` on the page, `dwell` tuned to settle exactly there |

A page with three peaks has none — demote the losers (shorter span, plainer
device). The close must resolve, not trail off: the divider collapses, the
world lands somewhere, the type quiets — never a fade to an empty stage.

## The tell-someone test

Complete, before building: *"it's the site where ___."* "It has a scrub
video" is a device name — no hook. "You drag the letters of the logo apart
and they snap back perfectly" is an experience — that's a hook. The blank has
to be something that happened **to the visitor**. This sentence usually
contains the signature move; if the tell-someone sentence and the signature
move point at different moments, one of them is decoration.

## The signature move

One bespoke interaction that exists on this build alone — coded in the page
off `--sc-p` or a page-authored `data-sc-*`, never a parameter on a kit
device, never in any prior build. The engine stays untouched.

**What counts** (upstream examples, not a menu to pick from): scroll-as-
playhead over a persistent trace rail; a wordmark the pointer pulls apart and
snaps back exactly; a line drawing whose `stroke-dashoffset` is driven from
`--sc-p`; a running receipt that accumulates real figures; one control that
regrades the whole page at once (time-of-day, temperature, load).

**What does not count**: a recoloured/resized spotlight; `data-sc-tilt` turned
up; a different easing on kinetic lines; more cards in a rail; a third
`scrub` act; anything the engine already does under a project class name.
Test: describe the move to someone who has seen the other builds — if they
can't tell it apart from something the kit already does, it isn't one.

## Being in it, not watching it

Upstream `feel.md` § 4. *"A film plays whether you are there or not. The
difference between a viewer and a participant is whether the page acknowledges
that somebody specific is here: how fast they are moving, where their pointer
is, whether they stopped."*

Five techniques, in the kit's own vocabulary:

- **Pointer parallax that moves the world, not a card.** `data-sc-spotlight`
  publishes `--sc-mx` / `--sc-my`. Drive a *background layer's* transform off
  them instead of a highlight, and the environment shifts as the visitor
  moves, slightly, the way a real space does when you lean.
- **Dwell-triggered detail.** Hold still on an act and something further
  arrives — a caption, a second line, a small annotation. Reward for stopping.
  Mechanically: **read `--sc-p` staying constant across a few frames**, in the
  page's own JS, and reveal something that was **never needed for
  comprehension**.
- **Scroll velocity shaping intensity.** Fast scrolling raises grain, blur,
  chromatic offset, ground saturation; slow scrolling settles it. *"The page
  feels like it is being driven rather than played back, and it costs one
  derived custom property."*
- **The page addressing "you" at one moment that lands.** Not throughout,
  which is just copywriting. **One line**, at the emotional turn, in second
  person, when the visitor is already implicated. *"It works because it is the
  only time."*
- **A trace of where they have been.** Anything that accumulates as they
  travel, so arriving at the end means having a record rather than reaching a
  footer.

**Embodiment is seasoning. One or two per page.** *"A page that reacts to
everything feels haunted, not alive: the visitor stops reading and starts
poking, which is the opposite of what any of this is for."* Pick the one that
serves the peak and leave the rest.

These are gated to `(hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)` — a pointer-capability
query, which stands.
Upstream also turns them off under reduced motion — **that half utgår, F-011**.
The rule that does survive is upstream's own:
*"a technique that only exists on desktop cannot be the thing that carries the
page's meaning."*

## Pacing as emotion

Upstream `feel.md` § 5. *"Scroll distance is emotional time. It is the only
clock this medium has, and it is fully under your control, which makes it the
cheapest emotional instrument in the kit and the one most often left at
default."*

| Pacing | Reads as | Built with |
|---|---|---|
| Short acts, hard cuts | Adrenaline, pulse, impatience | Acts under 1.4 vh, no `pin`, `dwell` at 0 |
| A long pin | Held breath, pressure, attention | `data-sc-span` 3+, overlapping cues, one idea |
| An empty viewport before a reveal | Silence before the drop | A ground-only act, no cue until the next one |
| A slow settle mid-act | The shot landing | `data-sc-dwell` 0.35–0.6, cue peak on the settle |
| A fast cue with a long plateau | Confidence, arrival | `data-sc-cue="0.1 0.9 0.08 0.4"` |
| A slow ramp in | Hesitation, dawning | Long `rampIn` — **once per page**, it is close to feeling broken |

Four rules follow:

- **Silence must be authored, not left over.** *"An empty screen you meant
  reads as anticipation. An empty screen you did not mean reads as a page that
  failed to load, and the harness reports both as dead scroll."* If the empty
  viewport before the peak is deliberate, **say so in `BRIEF.md`** so the
  verification pass can tell it from dead scroll. This is the sentence that
  keeps `scroll_verify.py`'s `blankBands` check from being either useless or a
  false alarm.
- **Give the peak room.** The peak act has the largest span on the page by a
  visible margin. *"If every act is 2.2 vh, the page has no shape, whatever
  the curve in BRIEF.md says."*
- **Compress the administrative parts.** Specs, logistics, FAQ, credentials
  are information, not experience — flow sections at short stagger, never
  pinned acts with dwell. Spending scroll on them spends the visitor's
  patience on the part they will not remember.
- **A continuous world is the exception to pacing variety.** All of the above
  is about a page of *acts*. A worldflight is one camera move, and *"a camera
  that changes speed between legs reads as broken rather than as
  expressive."* There, hold one pace and let the peak carry the shape by being
  the single long leg — [`pace.md`](pace.md).

The total-length budget stays **8–14 viewport-heights**. Pacing is how that
budget is spent, not permission to spend more: *"a page that needs 20 vh to
land its curve has too many acts, not too little room."*

## The fingerprint gate

Registry: `VAULT/wiki/projects/_index/design-fingerprints.md`, per-vault,
starting from whatever rows already exist — not repeating **yourself** across
builds, not a universal constraint. **Six dimensions**, recorded per row:

| # | Dimension | What it records |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Grammar | Which of `grammars.md`, or a named new one |
| 2 | Nav treatment | What the chrome is and what it's for |
| 3 | Hero device | What the first screen does |
| 4 | Act-sequence shape | Device order, act count, total viewport-heights |
| 5 | Close pattern | How the last screen behaves, what the CTA sits in |
| 6 | Signature move | The one bespoke interaction, in a phrase |

**The gate: a new build must differ from EVERY existing row on at least 4 of
the 6** — four against each row individually, not averaged across the table.
Dimension 6 is free (unique by definition), so the gate really asks for 3
more out of the remaining 5 against each row. If the plan fails, **change
the plan, not the log** — rewriting a row to fit is what makes it worthless.

**Row format** — one row per shipped build, all six dimensions plus a world
note and the path: `| Build | Grammar | Nav | Hero device | Act-sequence
shape | Close pattern | Signature move | Register | World / palette | Path |`

**Rows are append-only.** From upstream `templates/FINGERPRINTS.md`:

> *"A build that has been superseded stays in the table, because the space it
> occupies is still occupied."*

A replaced, retired or rejected build keeps its row. The registry does not
record what is live; it records what surface has already been taken, and a
surface stays taken whether or not the build that claimed it is still up.
Deleting a row silently frees a shape for reuse, which is the same failure as
editing one to make room — *"never edit a row to make room for it. If a
planned build fails, change the plan."*

**Fill every column.** A row with blanks cannot be scored 4-of-6 against, so
it weakens the gate for every build after it.

**Keep a "what is taken" list beside the table.** Add a bullet whenever a
build claims something a later build should avoid reusing: a grammar, a nav
treatment, a close pattern, a signature move, an act-count-and-length band.
*"The shared columns are what the next build inherits as a constraint, so
writing them down is the whole point."*

After shipping, append the row and say what it shares with prior rows — the
shared columns are exactly what the *next* build has to avoid.

# Design fingerprint registry

The fingerprint gate for scroll-choreographed Persuade/Experience builds. See
`.agents/skills/design/references/scroll/feel-and-fingerprint.md` § The
fingerprint gate for the rule: **a new build must differ from EVERY existing
row on at least 4 of the 6 dimension columns**, checked row by row, not
averaged across the table. If a planned build fails the gate, change the
plan, not this file — rewriting a row to make a new build fit is the one
thing that makes this registry worthless.

Seeded 2026-09-03 with one row per existing example site in
`anti-slop-design/sites/`. These sites predate scroll-craft integration and
were not built against the nine-device kit or the eight named grammars — the
Grammar, Signature move and Register columns below are an honest read of what
each page actually does, mapped onto scroll-craft's vocabulary after the
fact, not a claim that they were built to it. Where a site has no bespoke
interaction beyond an ordinary reveal-on-scroll, the Signature move column
says `none` — that is a finding, not a gap in the audit.

## Reading this table before a new build

Three grammar collisions already exist among these seven rows: Calyx,
Hyperborea and Vintergatan all read as chaptered editorial, and Vinterspelen
leans the same way with a gallery inflection. A new chaptered-editorial build
has to clear 3 more dimensions against **each** of those four rows
individually — nav treatment and hero device are the two that repeat across
them most (folio/edition-strip nav, type-in-photo or split-poster heroes), so
those are the columns most likely to collide again. Hōrai and Tidvatten share
grammar (filmic one-shot), a fixed minimal bar, a JS-parallax full-bleed
hero, and a bell-curve-scrub pinned set-piece as their signature move's
underlying mechanism — a third filmic one-shot build with a scrub-driven
pinned set-piece would need a genuinely different mechanism for the move, not
just different numbers on screen, to clear dimension 6 meaningfully even
though the gate counts it as free.

`before-ai-slop.html` is not a build to avoid colliding with — it is the
negative reference. Any real build should differ from it on every dimension
by construction.

## Alunix concept builds, rounds 1–7 (appended 2026-09-09)

Twenty-nine rows, one per built `index.html` under `anti-slop-design/tests/alunix-*`.
Every column is derived from the cell's own files: the built HTML (nav markup, section
list, `data-sc-act` attributes, `:root` custom properties, font links), its `NOTES.md`
or `BRIEF.md`, and its desktop fold screenshot read as an image. Where a cell's own
files carry no evidence for a column, the cell says `?` rather than a guess — that is a
finding about the cell's documentation, not a licence to treat the dimension as free.

Duplicates were excluded, not counted twice: `alunix-ab-r6/board/cells/*` are byte-identical
copies of the seven r6 runs, `alunix-ab-r7/board/cells/K1-1` and `K2-1` are byte-identical
copies of r6 B-K1 and B-K2 placed on r7's comparison board, and
`alunix-concepts-r5/reference/V3-baseline` is a byte-identical copy of `V3-chain`.

Rounds 1–2 and 6 predate scroll-craft integration in those cells (no `data-sc-*` in the
markup); their act shapes are hand-rolled. Rounds 3–5 and 7 run the engine. In r6 and r7,
arm A is the Claude-native control (Anthropic's `frontend-design` system prompt, no skills,
no hooks) and arm B is this chain; `B-K1-nogate` is the r6 chain run where the gate never
fired, kept as its own row because it is a separate build.

26	## Why it works
27	
28	The page opens between two moving marquee tickers — a thin cream strip above
29	the nav ("THE SCENT OF EXPENSIVE HOBBIES IS HERE") and a bold red strip below
30	the hero ("THIS IS NOT A BEAUTY BRAND") — so the brand's attitude is stated in
31	motion before any product is shown. The hero photograph itself (a clay tennis
32	court, balls mid-bounce) has nothing to do with the product literally; it's
33	establishing a lifestyle register — leisure, expense, ritual — that the
34	condensed all-caps headline ("WELLNESS ROOTED IN RITUAL, ART, AND DROP
35	CULTURE") then names directly.
36	
37	One display face, Anton — extremely condensed, extremely bold — carries every
38	headline, ticker and section statement at consistent weight, so scale is the
39	only variable used for emphasis; nothing shifts in style, only in size. Body
40	copy and product data drop to a plain Inter, keeping the loud parts loud and
41	the informational parts quiet. Product cards run on a black ground with cream
42	frames, a red "on sale" flag, and product photography with visible packaging
43	copy (the products themselves are typeset like the site, condensed bold
44	labels) — so the packaging and the page share one visual system rather than
45	photography being the only brand touchpoint.
46

48	with archival-style photography and a direct, culturally specific statement
49	("EVEN WHILE SLEEPING, BLACK PEOPLE CANNOT REST") — copy doing real narrative
50	work rather than generic brand-voice copy, which is unusual enough in this
51	genre to be the site's strongest asset.

54

59	  tennis court says "expensive leisure" faster than a product shot would.

61	  so hierarchy comes entirely from size, keeping the whole page visually
62	  coherent even across very different section types.
63	- **Let real, specific, culturally-grounded copy carry a "why" section** —
64	  it reads as conviction, not as brand-voice filler.
65	- **Match product packaging typography to the site's own type system** so
66	  photography and page feel like one continuous brand object.

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
3. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
4. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
5. **Can it be one line?** One line.
6. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project. Two rungs work → take the
higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the right one.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications with a `ponytail:` comment (`// ponytail: this exists`), simple reads as intent, not ignorance. Shortcut with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic)? The comment names the ceiling and the upgrade path: `# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`.

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.

Den här prompten är bara dispensern."* - Cell V3d, output dir `tests/alunix-r8/runs/V3d`, **port 3304**. - R23 built plan 067 in full. **"Stämpelrutan fungerar och rörs inte."** The two-column act, case chapter, price and contact section are built and **must not be rolled back**. - Anton's verdict on R23: *"Alla punkter från beställningen syns är gjorda … och resten av ändringarna motsvarade inte riktigt heller mina förväntningar även om de utfördes på papper."* — **"Avbockade punkter är inte samma sak som nådd nivå. Det är målet."** His feedback verbatim, image by image: `tests/alunix-r8/runs/V3d/HANDOFF-2026-09-20.md` § 3. - **"Läs i små stycken."** Large tool responses have felled this round twice. The nine faults (R24-BRIEF.md, 175 lines, re-read verbatim in full): 1. `--tx` unregistered custom property → `NaN` silently becoming 0. **Laid** (lines 258–260; must not be repeated). 2. `.tes-plane`'s fill is lighter than the accent from the start; for `tx ≤ 0.75` it must be **exactly `var(--c-accent)`**. Built, **unverified** — may already be solved by fel 1. "Mät, anta inte." 3. 46 of 121 frames under 18 % text area. The case ingress is still slop. **Not started.** "Skriv inte en tredje variant på samma stans — kundens situation eller ingen rad alls." 8. Run each **against the current (broken) state first** so you see it finds the fault. "En kontroll som ger grönt mot både trasigt och lagat mäter ingenting — det har hänt tre gånger i det här projektet." - "**Rapportera i renderat, inte i bytes.** Att strängen finns i filen eller i svaret över HTTP är inte ett bevis. Beviset är en **renderad bild av den sida Anton öppnar**, läst som bild." - "Enskilda skärmbilder, aldrig kontaktark som bevis. Chromium med `ignore_default_args=['--hide-scrollbars']`, `mouse.wheel`, en skärmbild per sida." - Short gate: 0 horizontal scroll 320–1920, 0 JS errors, the heading script, locked copy. - "**Kör därefter hela plan 067 § Verification A/B/C** (`tests/alunix-r8/runs/V3d/plans/067-*.md`), som R23 aldrig hann med på grund av full disk. Det är den körningen som avgör om R23 plus R24 kan kallas klara." Delivery: `tests/alunix-r8/runs/V3d/NOTES.md` § V3d R24 with **one table per fault: mål, före, efter, bild**. Key Technical Concepts: - CSS `@property` registration of unitless numeric custom properties (`syntax:""; inherits:true; initial-value:0`) — unregistered properties return a token stream, so `parseFloat` yields `NaN`, which silently becomes 0 in filters and comparisons. Reads are logged per-session, so the reads must be made with the Read tool in this session. `armed(root)` (design_hook_lib.py:308–314) checks `session_file(root, ARMED_NAME).exists()` or `FORCE_ARM_ENV`. The shell-write path (264–276) denies redirect/heredoc/tee/`sed -i`/`Set-Content`/`Out-File` when the session is armed, but explicitly allows `cp`/`mv`. `_check_reference_floor(root)` ends with `L.deny(msg)` unconditionally (design-gate.py lines 198–199). - **Scroll device kit (from `scroll/devices.md`, read this session):** nine devices — `scrub` (≤2/page, span 2.2–3.0 for a hero), `pin` (span ≥1.2), `pan` (rail `data-sc-pan="0.08"`, ~1vh per item + 1, overflow must be measured not assumed: `rail.scrollWidth - innerWidth`), `reveal` (`clip-path` wipe, `iris` once per page max), `kinetic` (lines almost always right, chars ~never, one per act), `parallax` (rate is **hundreds of px total travel**, usable 0.3–1.5 framed / 1–2 full-bleed, never on body copy, ≤3 layers), `count` (only real numbers, 1.2–1.8s outside an act), `flow`+`in` (stagger 30–80ms, fires once, opacity + 14px rise, ~620ms ease-out), pointer `tilt` (5–9°) / `magnet` (0.2–0.35, CTA only) / `spotlight` (publishes `--sc-mx`/`--sc-my`), gated to `(hover:hover) and (pointer:fine)`. **Cue contract** `data-sc-cue="from [to [rampIn [rampOut]]]"`: `"0.2"` fades in and holds; `"0.1 0.6"` in/plateau/out; `"0 0.78 0"` greet; `"0 1 0 0"` greet-and-hold. **The plateau is the point.** Five cue rules: a hero cue needs the greet form; the last act's cue must hold; only the last act may hold; ground or greet; clip time ≠ cue time. **The playhead is lerped** — scroll writes a target, a standalone rAF loop walks the clip toward it at lerp 0.18/frame (`data-sc-lerp` overrides, clamped 0.02–1, never 0), deadband 8 ms desktop / 20 ms mobile, seek coalescing. Upstream's reduced-motion branch "does not port: F-011". **Layered scenes §6:** plane rates differ 10–30 %, copy always at 1×; planes carry `max-width: none` and a fixed pixel width; never `transition: transform` on a parallaxed element (opacity only); new art gets a new name. **Premium fade-in §8** table (opacity 0→1, rise ~14 px, duration ~620 ms ease-out, stagger 30–80 ms, trigger IntersectionObserver `-12%` bottom root margin, fires once); *"Larger, slower, or bouncier is never more premium; the restraint is the signal."*; "A flow section directly after a pinned act takes reduced padding". **Rail settle §3:** exempt the first item, floor opacity ~0.55. **§9 devices that cannot share an element:** magnet, parallax and cue all write `transform`; 26	## Why it works
27	
28	Palette and type are read from Refero's extracted tokens, confirmed by the
29	live capture. Taupe paper `#ada59b` is not a "canvas colour" in the usual
30	sense — it is the entire site: the source states no section ever changes
31	background, so there is no light/dark alternation, no card surface, nothing
32	but one monolithic warm gray that every element floats on directly. Because
33	white, off-white and near-black are all explicitly forbidden as backgrounds,
34	photography becomes the only source of colour or contrast variation on the
35	whole page.
36	
37	Typography stays deliberately tiny across every functional role — 11-13px
38	WorkSans for navigation, labels, and body, with an explicit rule against ever
39	scaling up "for a primary label." That restraint is what makes the one
40	exception, the SilkSerif wordmark at 23px with letter-spacing opened to
41	0.5-0.8em, read as a masthead rather than a logo: the letters are so widely
42	tracked they nearly detach from each other, and because nothing else on the
43	page is set in serif, that single word instantly reads as the title plate of
44	a magazine.
45	
46	The image field is the structural centrepiece: photographs are placed with
47	irregular margin offsets (101-209px) rather than on a grid, so the layout
48	reads as a scattered contact sheet, not a portfolio grid. A working
49	LINEAR/RANDOM toggle — the only rounded (9999px) element in the entire
50	system — lets a viewer switch between an ordered and a scattered arrangement
51	of the same images, making the "contact sheet" metaphor an actual, operable
52	feature rather than just a visual style. Note: the designlang extract flags a
53	red `#dc3545` (31 uses, Bootstrap's default "danger" hue) not present in the
54	captured screenshot or documented anywhere in the source — most plausibly an
55	incidental form-validation or "sold out"-style state colour triggered during
56	the crawl rather than a deliberate brand accent, so it is not added to the
57	palette above; the exact taupe hex also reads slightly differently live
58	(`#e5ddc4`, `#a2a093`) than in the captured tokens, consistent with warm-gray
59	sampling variance rather than a different brand colour.
60	
61	## What to borrow (principle)
62	
63	- **Make the canvas a single, unchanging surface across the entire site.**
64	  Refusing section-to-section colour changes forces every other design
65	  decision (spacing, scatter, photography) to carry the visual rhythm
66	  instead.
67	- **Cap UI text size with an explicit rule, not just a habit.** "Never scale
68	  up for a primary label" keeps a whisper-small system from eroding under
69	  the pressure to make one thing "important."
70	- **Reserve the one rounded shape for exactly one interactive feature.**
71	  A 9999px pill appearing only on a working layout toggle — nowhere else —
72	  makes that single curve meaningful rather than decorative.
73	- **Offer a genuinely operable metaphor, not just a visual one.** A real
74	  LINEAR/RANDOM toggle that rearranges the same photographs turns "contact
75	  sheet" from a style reference into an interactive feature.
76	- **Open tracking on a masthead word until letters nearly detach.** Extreme
77	  positive letter-spacing (0.5-0.8em) on a short serif word is what makes a
78	  wordmark read as a printed title rather than a typed logo.
79	
80	## What to leave
81	
82	- A monolithic single-colour canvas with zero section variation is a
83	  demanding constraint — any content type that needs visual separation (a
84	  pricing table, a form) has no built-in surface-shift tool to reach for.
85	- Irregular image offsets (101-209px, scattered) require genuine art
86	  direction per breakpoint; a naive responsive collapse would either overlap
87	  badly or lose the contact-sheet read entirely.
88	- Zero accent colour anywhere means the system offers no built-in way to
89	  signal state (hover beyond a colour swap to pure ink, active, error)
90	  without inventing a convention from scratch.
91	
92	## Signature move
93	
94	The LINEAR/RANDOM layout toggle: a stroke-only pill switch that rearranges
95	the same scattered photographs between an ordered and a randomized
96	composition — the only rounded, only interactive-feeling component on the
97	entire site, and the one place the "contact sheet" concept becomes literally
98	operable.
99	
100	## Motion
101	
102	(from designlang extract) Feel reads as mixed, and the page is scroll-linked.
103	Four durations are confirmed — 200ms, 300ms, 1s and a notably slow 2s — though
104	no easing curve is confidently identified (no dominant named family
105	registers). That wide spread, especially the 2s outlier, fits a genuinely
106	deliberate grid-rearrange animation: images repositioning across the scattered
107	field when the LINEAR/RANDOM toggle fires would plausibly need a slower,
108	choreographed duration rather than a snap cut. No keyframes are confirmed
109	firing. (observed in capture) the live capture confirms the scattered,
110	irregularly-offset image field and the LINEAR/RANDOM toggle are present and
111	match the described layout.
112	
113	| Token | Value | Easing |
114	|---|---|---|
115	| sm | 200ms | — |
116	| md | 300ms | — |
117	| xl | 1s | — |
118	| xxl (toggle rearrange) | 2s | — |
119	
120	## Brief
121	
122	Build a Copenhagen-style creative-studio portfolio with a single unchanging
123	canvas. Set the entire page on warm taupe `#ada59b` — no section, card, or
124	component ever uses a different background; white, off-white and near-black
125	are all forbidden as surfaces. Cap all UI text (nav, labels, body, metadata)
126	at 11-13px WorkSans Regular — never scale up for emphasis. Set the studio
127	name in a light serif at 23px with letter-spacing opened to 0.5-0.8em, tight
128	0.94 leading, centred in the top bar as the only serif moment on the site.
129	Arrange 6-8 photographs in an asymmetric scattered field with irregular
130	margin offsets (roughly 100-210px), each at 0px radius with no border or
131	shadow, ringed by floating uppercase category labels positioned at irregular
132	coordinates (top-left, top-centre, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-centre,
133	bottom-right). Add a working LINEAR/RANDOM toggle — a stroke-only 9999px
134	pill with a small circular thumb, the only rounded element anywhere — that
135	rearranges the image field between ordered and scattered layouts. Centre a
136	single studio-statement paragraph below at 13px with generous (180px) top
137	padding. No accent colour, no shadows, no elevation anywhere.
138	
139	## Image recipe
140	
141	Editorial documentary photograph of [SUBJECT] — packaging, interior, product-
142	on-table or portrait-detail shots at high resolution, warm and slightly
143	desaturated, lit naturally rather than in a studio, cropped tight at varying
144	aspect ratios (1:1, 4:5, 3:2) so the collection reads as a contact sheet
145	rather than a uniform grid.
146	
147	## Photo search
148	
149	Unsplash first, Pexels second.
150	- "editorial product photography warm natural light"
151	- "interior photography natural light desaturated"
152	- "packaging design close up studio"
153	- "portrait detail natural light editorial"
154	
155	## Reference lock
156	
157	Primary reference/direction: ALET Agency — single-surface taupe portfolio,
158	scattered contact-sheet image field, whisper-small caption typography.
159	Preserve (3-5 traits): warm taupe `#ada59b` as the entire site's only
160	background, never white/off-white/near-black; all UI text capped at 11-13px
161	WorkSans, no scaling up for emphasis; the SilkSerif masthead at 23px with
162	0.5-0.8em tracking as the only serif moment; photographs at irregular
163	scattered offsets (not gridded), 0px radius, no border or shadow; 9999px
164	radius reserved exclusively for the LINEAR/RANDOM toggle.
165	Borrow only (1-2): the working LINEAR/RANDOM layout toggle that rearranges
166	the same image set; the floating category-label positioning around the
167	image field.
168	Role rules: no chromatic accent is ever introduced; the wordmark's letter-
169	spacing formula (0.5-0.8em) never applies to body or nav text; body text
170	never centres except the single studio-statement block.
171	Media strategy: photo:unsplash — warm, naturally-lit editorial documentary
172	photography at varying tight crops; no illustration, no icons beyond fine
173	line-art strokes.
174	Reject: any second background colour; box-shadow or gradient; radius above
175	0px outside the toggle and rare small inset frames; a display weight above
176	Light/Regular; a centred multi-column body layout.
177	Token commitments: bg `#ada59b`, ink `#000000`, nav-text `#252525`,
178	secondary `#101010`, inset `#454545`; wordmark SilkSerif 300 at 23px/leading
179	0.94/0.5-0.8em tracking; body WorkSans 400 at 11-13px/leading 1.0-1.5;
180	radius 0px images, 9999px toggle only, 10.8px rare small frames; section gap
181	101-180px, base spacing unit 6px.

PONYTAIL MODE ACTIVE — level: full

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
3. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
4. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
5. **Can it be one line?** One line.
6. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project. Two rungs work → take the
higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the right one.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications with a `ponytail:` comment (`// ponytail: this exists`), simple reads as intent, not ignorance. Shortcut with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic)? The comment names the ceiling and the upgrade path: `# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`.

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.

25	
26	## Why it works
27	
28	The hero is competent, generic-good: a real modern house photographed at dusk,
29	warm interior light glowing against a cooling sky, a plain two-line claim
30	("Harmony shaped by light, material, and space") and a small "[SCROLL DOWN]"
31	cue. Nothing here is wrong — it's the correct recipe for an architecture-studio
32	hero, warm light against cool sky, plain confident copy, a registered wordmark.
33	
34	The interesting failure shows up in the "about" copy just below the fold, which
35	drifts, mid-paragraph, from architecture language into unrelated software
36	language: "every detail we design — from a color system to a dashboard
37	layout — is rooted in user behavior..." A studio it claims to have "founded
38	with a vision to craft spaces" is, one sentence later, talking about ensuring
39	"every product scales beautifully, performs seamlessly across platforms." This
40	is copy written for a SaaS product, pasted into an architecture template
41	without being reread — a genuine tell of templated or AI-generated content that
42	never got a human edit pass.
43	
44	Everything else on the page follows the category's honest defaults: a paired
45	interior-photo-plus-portrait "about" block, and a four-stat achievement row
46	(`95+ Curated Interiors`, `7 Years of Expertise`...). It's a useful reference
47	precisely because it shows how far competent visual defaults can carry a page
48	even when the copy underneath them has stopped meaning anything specific.
49	
50	## What to borrow (principle)
51	
52	- **Photograph real work at dusk**, warm interior light against a cooling sky —
53	  it's a reliable, flattering register for architecture and interior work.
54	- **Pair a portrait of the designer with an interior photograph** in the "about"
55	  block, so the studio has a human face, not just a body of work.
56	- **State achievement stats as a plain four-number row** directly after the
57	  "about" copy, as concrete follow-through on the claim just made.
58	
59	## What to leave
60	
61	- Copy that drifts from the stated category (architecture) into unrelated
62	  vocabulary (color systems, dashboards, "scales beautifully... across
63	  platforms") within the same paragraph — this is the single clearest tell
64	  that content was templated or generated without a domain-specific edit pass,
65	  and it undermines every other well-executed choice on the page.
66	- A registered-trademark symbol on a studio wordmark with no other markers of
67	  an established, litigation-aware brand reads as borrowed gravitas rather than
68	  earned.
69	
70	## Signature move
71	
72	Not a device worth reusing — the notable "move" here is a cautionary one: the
73	about-section copy silently swaps industries mid-paragraph, moving from spatial
74	design language to software-product language without the switch being
75	acknowledged or corrected. It's the page's most instructive feature precisely
76	because it's a mistake.
77	
78	## Motion
79	
80	(from designlang extract) Feel is "mixed" with scroll-linked motion confirmed,
81	though the captured CSS is minimal — a single `1ms` allow-discrete overflow
82	transition and a bare `transition: all`, with only a generic loading-spinner
83	keyframe present. No scroll-prompt animation on the "[SCROLL DOWN]" cue was
84	captured; that read stays inferred from the image, consistent with this being
85	a template whose content (see Why it works) also wasn't fully finished.
86	
87	| token | value | role |
88	|---|---|---|
89	| `instant` | 1ms | framework overflow transition |
90	
91	## Brief
92	
93	If borrowing this direction: keep the dusk architectural hero, the paired
94	portrait-plus-interior "about" block, and the four-stat achievement row — all
95	genuinely solid defaults for the category. Replace the about-section copy
96	entirely with language specific to the actual practice (materials, process,
97	typology, geography) and have it read by someone who would notice a stray
98	"dashboard layout" or "scales across platforms" reference before it ships.
99	Never let generic or copy-pasted template language survive into a page whose
100	whole pitch is bespoke, considered craft.
101	
102	## Image recipe
103	
104	A modern architectural [SUBJECT] photographed at dusk, warm interior light
105	glowing through glazing against a cooling blue-grey sky, wide establishing
106	shot with the building's full form visible, natural landscaping in the
107	foreground, no visible people.
108	
109	## Photo search
110	
111	Unsplash first, Pexels second.
112	- "modern house dusk warm light exterior"
113	- "architecture twilight glass facade"
114	- "residential building blue hour warm windows"
115	
116	## Reference lock
117	
118	Primary reference/direction: Archline — dusk architectural photography hero with a paired portrait/interior about-section, undermined by mismatched template copy.
119	Preserve (3-5 traits): dusk photography of real completed work, warm interior light against a cooling sky; a paired designer-portrait-plus-interior-photo "about" block; a plain four-stat achievement row directly following the about copy; a plain two-line claim in the hero with a scroll-down cue.
120	Borrow only (1-2): the registered-trademark wordmark treatment, only if the brand is genuinely established; the small "[SCROLL DOWN]" cue.
121	Role rules: every paragraph of body copy must stay within the stated practice's actual vocabulary — no cross-industry language may survive an edit pass; stats must be real and verifiable, not template placeholders.
122	Media strategy: photo:unsplash — dusk, warm-lit architectural photography of real (or realistic) completed work only; portraits must be genuine or plausibly genuine, not generic stock "professional headshot" imagery.
123	Reject: shipping copy that drifts between unrelated industries within a paragraph; unverified achievement stats; a registered-trademark mark on an unestablished brand.
124	Token commitments: dusk-blue `#4A5A6E`, warm-amber `#D9A860`, paper `#F2EEE6`, ink `#1D1B18`, stone `#8B8577`; plain sans for all type.

## Why it works

The hero is competent, generic-good: a real modern house photographed at dusk,
warm interior light glowing against a cooling sky, a plain two-line claim
("Harmony shaped by light, material, and space") and a small "[SCROLL DOWN]"
cue. Nothing here is wrong — it's the correct recipe for an architecture-studio
hero, warm light against cool sky, plain confident copy, a registered wordmark.

The interesting failure shows up in the "about" copy just below the fold, which
drifts, mid-paragraph, from architecture language into unrelated software
language: "every detail we design — from a color system to a dashboard
layout — is rooted in user behavior..." A studio it claims to have "founded
with a vision to craft spaces" is, one sentence later, talking about ensuring
"every product scales beautifully, performs seamlessly across platforms." This
is copy written for a SaaS product, pasted into an architecture template
without being reread — a genuine tell of templated or AI-generated content that
never got a human edit pass.

Everything else on the page follows the category's honest defaults: a paired
interior-photo-plus-portrait "about" block, and a four-stat achievement row
(`95+ Curated Interiors`, `7 Years of Expertise`...). It's a useful reference
precisely because it shows how far competent visual defaults can carry a page
even when the copy underneath them has stopped meaning anything specific.

## What to borrow (principle)

- **Photograph real work at dusk**, warm interior light against a cooling sky —
  it's a reliable, flattering register for architecture and interior work.
- **Pair a portrait of the designer with an interior photograph** in the "about"
  block, so the studio has a human face, not just a body of work.
- **State achievement stats as a plain four-number row** directly after the
  "about" copy, as concrete follow-through on the claim just made.

## What to leave

- Copy that drifts from the stated category (architecture) into unrelated
  vocabulary (color systems, dashboards, "scales beautifully... across
  platforms") within the same paragraph — this is the single clearest tell
  that content was templated or generated without a domain-specific edit pass,
  and it undermines every other well-executed choice on the page.
- A registered-trademark symbol on a studio wordmark with no other markers of
  an established, litigation-aware brand reads as borrowed gravitas rather than
  earned.

## Signature move

Not a device worth reusing — the notable "move" here is a cautionary one: the
about-section copy silently swaps industries mid-paragraph, moving from spatial
design language to software-product language without the switch being
acknowledged or corrected. It's the page's most instructive feature precisely
because it's a mistake.

## Motion

(from designlang extract) Feel is "mixed" with scroll-linked motion confirmed,
though the captured CSS is minimal — a single `1ms` allow-discrete overflow
transition and a bare `transition: all`, with only a generic loading-spinner
keyframe present. No scroll-prompt animation on the "[SCROLL DOWN]" cue was
captured; that read stays inferred from the image, consistent with this being
a template whose content (see Why it works) also wasn't fully finished.

| token | value | role |
|---|---|---|
| `instant` | 1ms | framework overflow transition |

## Brief

If borrowing this direction: keep the dusk architectural hero, the paired
portrait-plus-interior "about" block, and the four-stat achievement row — all
genuinely solid defaults for the category. Replace the about-section copy
entirely with language specific to the actual practice (materials, process,
typology, geography) and have it read by someone who would notice a stray
"dashboard layout" or "scales across platforms" reference before it ships.
Never let generic or copy-pasted template language survive into a page whose
whole pitch is bespoke, considered craft.

## Image recipe

A modern architectural [SUBJECT] photographed at dusk, warm interior light
glowing through glazing against a cooling blue-grey sky, wide establishing
shot with the building's full form visible, natural landscaping in the
foreground, no visible people.

## Photo search

Unsplash first, Pexels second.
- "modern house dusk warm light exterior"
- "architecture twilight glass facade"
- "residential building blue hour warm windows"

## Reference lock

Primary reference/direction: Archline — dusk architectural photography hero with a paired portrait/interior about-section, undermined by mismatched template copy.
Preserve (3-5 traits): dusk photography of real completed work, warm interior light against a cooling sky; a paired designer-portrait-plus-interior-photo "about" block; a plain four-stat achievement row directly following the about copy; a plain two-line claim in the hero with a scroll-down cue.
Borrow only (1-2): the registered-trademark wordmark treatment, only if the brand is genuinely established; the small "[SCROLL DOWN]" cue.
Role rules: every paragraph of body copy must stay within the stated practice's actual vocabulary — no cross-industry language may survive an edit pass; stats must be real and verifiable, not template placeholders.
Media strategy: photo:unsplash — dusk, warm-lit architectural photography of real (or realistic) completed work only; portraits must be genuine or plausibly genuine, not generic stock "professional headshot" imagery.
Reject: shipping copy that drifts between unrelated industries within a paragraph; unverified achievement stats; a registered-trademark mark on an unestablished brand.
Token commitments: dusk-blue `#4A5A6E`, warm-amber `#D9A860`, paper `#F2EEE6`, ink `#1D1B18`, stone `#8B8577`; plain sans for all type.

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
3. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
4. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
5. **Can it be one line?** One line.
6. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project. Two rungs work → take the
higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the right one.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications with a `ponytail:` comment (`// ponytail: this exists`), simple reads as intent, not ignorance. Shortcut with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic)? The comment names the ceiling and the upgrade path: `# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`.

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.

PONYTAIL MODE ACTIVE — level: full

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
3. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
4. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
5. **Can it be one line?** One line.
6. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project. Two rungs work → take the
higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the right one.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications with a `ponytail:` comment (`// ponytail: this exists`), simple reads as intent, not ignorance. Shortcut with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic)? The comment names the ceiling and the upgrade path: `# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`.

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.

Shortcut with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic)? The comment names the ceiling and the upgrade path: `# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`.

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.

PONYTAIL MODE ACTIVE — level: full

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
3. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
4. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
5. **Can it be one line?** One line.
6. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project. Two rungs work → take the
higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the right one.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications with a `ponytail:` comment (`// ponytail: this exists`), simple reads as intent, not ignorance. Shortcut with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic)? The comment names the ceiling and the upgrade path: `# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`.

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.

  @property --p-t    { syntax: "<number>"; inherits: false; initial-value: 0; }
  @property --p-thin { syntax: "<number>"; inherits: false; initial-value: 0; }
  @property --p-fill { syntax: "<number>"; inherits: false; initial-value: 0; }
  @property --p-fall { syntax: "<number>"; inherits: false; initial-value: 0; }

  /* R24 FEL 1 (kedjedisciplin M1). Varje numerisk custom property som ett
     skript, ett prov eller en granskare LÄSER maste vara registrerad.
     Oregistrerad ar vardet en tokenstrom - getPropertyValue('--tx') gav
     "clamp(0,calc((0.3205 - 0.2258) / 0.1613),1)", parseFloat gav NaN, och
     NaN blir tyst 0 i varje filter och varje if. Samma falla gjorde
     --slit-p-filtret verkningslost i r18 OCH i Astras r21- och r22-korning,

     inherits:true - de ar alla lästa av ÄTTLINGAR (.tes-plane/.seam/

     INTE --x1, --x2, --x3, --x4, --sx1..4, --pl-t, --pl-r, --pl-l eller
     --dn: de bär px, en <number>-registrering hade gjort dem ogiltiga och
     tystnat dem till 0.
     INTE --sc-ps: motorn registrerar den sjalv (sc-smooth.js
     CSS.registerProperty), och motorn rörs aldrig. */
  @property --tx     { syntax: "<number>"; inherits: true; initial-value: 0; }
  @property --cx     { syntax: "<number>"; inherits: true; initial-value: 0; }
  @property --slit-p { syntax: "<number>"; inherits: true; initial-value: 0; }

     ocksa vara registrerade. Deras initialvarden ar INTE 0: CSS:ns
     fallback ar var(--tx-a,.07)/var(--tx-b,.29), och en registrering med

     division med noll i --tx-formeln i varje bildruta innan measureAct
     hunnit skriva dem. Samma tal som fallbacken, sa beteendet ar identiskt
     fore och efter registreringen. */
  @property --tx-a   { syntax: "<number>"; inherits: true; initial-value: 0.07; }
  @property --tx-b   { syntax: "<number>"; inherits: true; initial-value: 0.29; }

  :focus-visible{outline:2px solid #f4f2ef;outline-offset:2px;}

  /* ============================================================ grunden
     Ett enda fotografi bär hela sidan. Fixed, gråskala, tonad av motorns
     --sc-canvas-drift i tre stopp. Ingen andra bakgrundsbild finns.
     background-attachment:fixed är BORTTAGET mot V3b: elementet är redan
     position:fixed, så attachmentet var en ren repaint-kostnad utan effekt. */
  /* Tonen ligger som ett eget bakgrundslager PÅ grunden och blandas med
     `background-blend-mode`, som bara blandar elementets egna lager, i stället
     för V3b:s `::after` i `mix-blend-mode: color`, som läser sidans backdrop.
     `transition: background 1.1s` är borttagen: motorn interpolerar redan
     --sc-canvas kontinuerligt, så transitionen målade om ett helskärmslager i
     1,1 s efter varje drift-steg utan att synas.

     contain:strict är MÄTT FRAM, inte gissad. Attribution vid 4x CPU,
     `motion_probe --wheel 100:60`, p95 i ms:
       som byggd .............................. 33,4
       utan filter ............................ 33,3   filtret var inte felet
       utan background-blend-mode ............. 33,4   blandningen var inte felet
       utan filter OCH blend .................. 33,3   inte heller tillsammans
       .ground display:none ................... 16,8   grunden ÄR felet
       .ground + will-change:transform ........ 33,4   promovering gör det VÄRRE
       .ground + contain:strict ............... 16,8   rätt verktyg
     Kostnaden var att ett helskärmsstort fast raster målades om per hjulhack,
     inte att det var filtrerat eller blandat. `contain: strict` är sant om det
     här elementet: storleken kommer ur inset:0 och inte ur innehållet, det har
     inga barn, och det målar bara i sin egen ruta. Raden är samtidigt belägget
     för performance.md:s förbud mot vilande `will-change`: promoveringen
     fördubblade antalet tappade bildrutor i stället för att ta bort dem. */
  /* PLAN 017 A: filter:grayscale(1) låg EFTER background-blend-mode:color,
     så tonen blandades in och togs sedan bort av gråskalan innan den nådde
     skärmen (driften var död av konstruktion, mätt 25,25,25 = 25,25,25 vid
     folden mot tesen). Gråskalan flyttas till fotolagret (::before), tonen
     läggs ovanpå (::after) inne i .ground:s egen contain:strict-kontext. */
  .ground{position:fixed;inset:0;z-index:0;pointer-events:none;contain:strict;
    background:var(--c-black);}
  .ground::before{content:"";position:absolute;inset:0;
    background:var(--ground-img) center 40% / cover no-repeat;
    filter:grayscale(1) contrast(1.08) brightness(.5);}
  /* PLAN 029: 62 % färgade hela fotografiet blått (rännan bakom jätten
     mätte (58,86,111) mot gråskalans (80,80,80), leadens R7-fynd). Planens
     40 % (loop 2:s tal, delta 13) mätte här bara delta 10 (fold (19,20,21)
     mot tesen (12,22,31)) - under H-19:s 12-stegsgolv, sannolikt en annan
     färgprofil/Chrome-version än loop 2:s mätning. Planens egen fallback
     (steg 2: "faller det, höj till 44 %") tillämpad. */

     (color-blending skalar med luminansen) och är omskrivet i HELHET H-19. */
  .ground::after{content:"";position:absolute;inset:0;
    background:color-mix(in srgb,var(--sc-canvas) 24%,transparent);
    mix-blend-mode:color;}

    display:flex;align-items:center;justify-content:space-between;
    padding:16px var(--rail-x);}

  .topline-mark{font-weight:300;font-size:clamp(13px,1.6vw,17px);letter-spacing:.02em;color:#f4f2ef;}

    display:inline-flex;align-items:center;min-height:44px;padding-inline:4px;margin-inline:-4px;
    transition:border-color .25s var(--ease),color .25s var(--ease);}
  .topline-contact:hover{color:#f4f2ef;border-color:currentColor;}

     för seende ögon. */
  .sr-only{position:absolute;width:1px;height:1px;padding:0;margin:-1px;
    overflow:hidden;clip:rect(0 0 0 0);white-space:nowrap;border:0;}

     Ingenting nedan sätter position, height eller overflow på stagen.

     PLAN 003, R4. Den regeln höll inte helt: stagens HÖJD kom bara från
     `.sc-stage`, en klass motorn lägger på asynkront i `mount()`. Mätt med
     ett tidsspår vid 4x CPU: vid t=300 ms saknade `[data-sc-stage]` fortfarande
     `.sc-stage` och rymdes på sin naturliga innehållshöjd, 606 px vid 390.
     Vid t=500 ms hade `mount()` lagt till klassen och tvingat höjden till
     100svh, 844 px. Den centrerade flex-kolumnen (`justify-content:center`)
     skiftade då sitt innehåll neråt med hälften av mellanskillnaden, 119 px,
     exakt CLS-rapportens `figure.hero-plate`-hopp. Källan var alltså varken
     typsnitt (blockerade, CLS oförändrad) eller bilder, utan tajmingen
     mellan första målning och motorns eget klasstillägg.
     Fixen är att sätta SAMMA höjd på attributselektorn `[data-sc-stage]`,
     inte på klassen `.sc-stage` (AB06: motorns klasser restylas aldrig).
     Attributet finns i DOM:en från parse-tid, så höjden är 100svh redan vid
     första målningen, och `mount()`s klasstillägg ändrar ingenting som redan
     inte stod där. */
  [data-sc-stage]{height:100vh;height:100svh;}
  /* Innehållet centreras i stagen på ALLA bredder. Mätt i pixlar: vid
     1440x900 fyller folden stagen så när som på en pixel och centreringen
     ändrar ingenting, men vid 768x1024 låg 364 px död yta under underraden när
     innehållet var toppställt. Felet följer viewportens HÖJD, inte dess bredd,
     så regeln hör inte hemma i en breddbrytpunkt. */
  .hero-stage{display:flex;flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;
    padding:clamp(44px,5.6vh,64px) 0 clamp(6px,2.2vh,26px);}

  .hero-head{padding:0 var(--rail-x);}
  /* Rubriken ligger på den mörka GRUNDEN, aldrig över plåtens ljuspöl
     (planhat: vikt 300 i stor grad ligger i fotots mörka parti). Scrimmen är
     bunden till rubrikens eget block och är ett syskonlager, aldrig ett
     ::before på ett element shoot.mjs döljer. */
  .hero-head::before{content:"";position:absolute;left:0;right:0;top:0;height:52vh;z-index:-1;
    background:linear-gradient(180deg,rgba(5,6,7,.58) 0%,rgba(5,6,7,.38) 62%,rgba(5,6,7,0) 100%);
    pointer-events:none;}
  /* Taket höjt 7rem -> 7.5rem, se BRIEF.md § decision ledger rättelse 3:
     vid 1440 band 7rem vid 112 px och kvoten mot kortbaksidans 80,6 px blev
     0,72, över målet 0,70. 7.5rem = 120 px ger 0,67 och baksidan 5,04x
     brödtexten. Golvet sänkt 2.6rem -> 2.2rem för 320 px, se NOTES.md § R2. */
  /* PLAN 001, R4: bredd-klämman ensam gav ett tak som INTE följde
     viewporthöjden, bara viewportbredden (cqw). Vid breda men LÅGA viewports
     (1024-1440 x 450-640) blev rubriken 81-114 px oavsett hur lite höjd som
     fanns, och summan av padding + rubrik + plåt + underrad sprängde folden:
     mätt kollision mellan ordmärke och rubrik -85,9 px vid 1440x450, och
     underraden klippt 74,4 px under vecket.
     Fixen är en ANDRA klämma bunden till `--h1-hrate` (svh) och `min()` av de
     två: den som är strängast vinner. Se `--h1-hrate`-deklarationen i :root
     och brytpunkten nedan för varför raten själv byter värde vid 700 px. */
  /* PLAN 049 fix 8 (Astra material_fixes #8). Golvet 2.2rem->2.875rem
     (46px): 9cqw har ingen container-förfader (varken .hero-head eller
     någon av dess anor sätter container-type), så den faller tillbaka
     mot viewport-bredd - vid 390 ger det ~35px, UNDER det gamla golvet,
     så min() alltid valde golvet. Höjt golvet direkt i stället för att
     jaga cqw-uttrycket (som ändå faller tillbaka korrekt vid 1440,
     ~120px, oförändrat). */
  .hero-headline{font-family:var(--font);font-weight:300;
    font-size:min(clamp(2.875rem,9cqw,7.5rem), clamp(1.5rem,var(--h1-hrate),7.5rem));
    line-height:.96;letter-spacing:-.01em;
    color:#f7f5f0;max-width:15ch;text-wrap:balance;overflow-wrap:anywhere;min-width:0;}
  /* Den branta raten. Löst mot UPPMÄTTA element-höjder (fold_debug.py, se
     NOTES.md § R4), inte mot antagna: vid 1440x450 är underraden 68,4 px,
     plåten 252 px (0,56*450), ordmärkets nederkant 41,5 px, och toppradens
     padding-golv 44 px oförändrat (44 > 41,5, så det räcker för att fria
     ordmärket så snart summan inte längre svämmar över och tvingar
     centreringen att skjuta upp innehållet). 7,2svh ger rubriken 62,2 px
     (två rader) vid 450, vilket lämnar foldens summa 1,8 px under 450 i
     stället för 46,6 över. */
  @media (max-height:700px){ :root{ --h1-hrate:7.2svh; } }

  /* ---------------------------------------------------------- kortet
     Storleken är LÅST och oförändrad från V3b: 16:9, vänsteranknuten vid
     --rail-x, bredden härledd ur en höjdbudget så att rubrik + kort + underrad
     ryms i en fold. container-type gör att kortbaksidans 9cqw mäter mot
     PLÅTEN (896 px vid 1440) och inte mot sidan (1440 px). */
  /* INGEN bakgrund här. Mätt i R2: med background:#08090a låg en statisk svart
     rektangel kvar i plåtens fulla bredd medan kortet vändes inuti den, och det
     läste som ett litet kort i ett svart fönster i stället för som ett kort som
     vänds. Plåten är en osynlig ram; det enda som syns är kortet.
     overflow:clip står kvar: vid 63° sticker kortets närmaste kant 84 px utanför
     rutan i perspektiv, och utan klippning korsar den rubriken 12,6 px ovanför. */
  /* PLAN 022 Step 1, R6. Fokusen som parkeras hit (setFace) ska inte
     rita en egen ring: den är osynlig (tabindex=-1 tar bort den ur
     tabbordningen), bara ett programmatiskt stopp. Länkens egen ring
     räcker. */
  .hero-plate:focus{outline:none;}
  .hero-plate{position:relative;margin:clamp(4px,1.4vh,18px) var(--rail-x) 0;
    width:min(calc(100% - 2 * var(--rail-x)),calc(56vh * 16 / 9));
    aspect-ratio:16 / 9;
    container-type:inline-size;
    /* perspective höjd 1600 -> 2600: flackare projektion, mindre hörnutskjutning i
       vändningen. overflow:clip står kvar som skydd — folden är för tät (13 px till
       rubriken ovan, 11 px till underraden nedan) för att kortet ska få spilla ut.
       I stället KRYMPER kortet transient mitt i vändningen (se .plate-card scale),
       så dess perspektivprojektion aldrig når klippkanten och inget kapas. */
    perspective:2600px;
    overflow:clip;}

  /* Kortet självt. Rotationen räknas i ren CSS ur --sc-ps:
       t    = clamp(0, (ps - 0.10) / 0.68, 1)
       flip = t*t*(3 - 2t)                         (smoothstep 0.10 -> 0.78)
     ps 0 till 0,10: flip 0, kortet stilla medan ljuspölen vandrar.
     ps 0,10 till 0,78: vändningen.
     ps 0,78 till 1: flip 1, baksidan i vila, dwell låter den landa.
     Båda riktningarna, eftersom hela uttrycket är en funktion av ps.
     PLAN 011, R5: span 4,8 -> 3,4, dwell 0,35 -> 0,2, fönstret 0,12-0,72 ->
     0,10-0,78. Vändningen tar 1 469 px vid 1440x900 (0,68 x 2 160), svansen
     (baksidans vila + dwell) 655 px, mot tidigare 2 052 px + 1 273 px
     stillastående (scroll_verify: band 2700-3300 diff 0,0). */
  .plate-card{position:absolute;inset:0;
    --t:clamp(0,calc((var(--sc-ps,0) - 0.10) / 0.68),1);
    --flip:calc(var(--t) * var(--t) * (3 - 2 * var(--t)));
    transform-style:preserve-3d;
    /* Vändningen plus en transient nedskalning: parabeln 0.72*flip*(1-flip) är 0 vid
       flip 0 och 1 (kortet står i full, LÅST storlek fram och bak) och toppar på 0.18
       vid 90°, så kortet drar sig ~15-18% mindre mitt i vändningen. Mätt vid 1440x900:
       kortets projicerade hörn håller sig 7-11 px innanför plåten i hela spannet, så
       overflow:clip aldrig kapar en synlig yta. Ett kort som vänds drar sig naturligt
       undan; nedskalningen läser som djup, inte som en krympning. */
    transform:rotateY(calc(var(--flip,0) * -180deg))
              scale(calc(1 - 0.72 * var(--flip,0) * (1 - var(--flip,0))));}
  /* will-change bara medan akten rör sig. Klassen sätts och tas bort vid
     gränsövergång, inte per bildruta. */
  .hero.is-turning .plate-card{will-change:transform;}

  .face{position:absolute;inset:0;backface-visibility:hidden;
    border:1px solid var(--frame-line);overflow:clip;}
  .face--front{background:#08090a;}
  /* Väg (d) 1 ur ASSETS.md § 3: framsidan mörknar när planet vrider sig bort
     från ljuset, så fram- och baksida får olika värdekurva och mötet vid 90°
     blir en övergång i stället för ett klipp. Ren opacity, ingen filter. */
  .face--front::after{content:"";position:absolute;inset:0;background:var(--c-black);
    opacity:min(.65,calc(1.3 * var(--flip,0)));pointer-events:none;}
  .face--back{transform:rotateY(180deg);background:var(--c-black);}

  /* Ljuspölen vandrar vidare, på --sc-ps och i ren CSS.
     MÄTT I R2: den första versionen körde vandringen på `object-position`, som
     V3b gör. object-position är inte kompositerbar: varje bildruta ritade om en
     896x504 stor bild, och `motion_probe` gav p95 50 ms och 63 bildrutor över
     33 ms vid 4x CPU. Rörelsen är nu en `translate3d` på en bild som är 112 %
     av ytans höjd, med 6 % av sin egen höjd att vandra i. Samma vandring, samma
     motiv, samma riktning, men på kompositorn i stället för på målaren.
     object-fit:cover sköter passformen, så konstruktionen håller även när ytan
     blir 4:5 på telefonen. */
  .face--front img{position:absolute;left:0;top:-6%;width:100%;height:112%;
    object-fit:cover;object-position:50% 52%;
    transform:translate3d(0,calc(-3% + 6% * var(--sc-ps,0)),0);}

  /* Kortets egen tjocklek, hängd på den LEDANDE kanten. Mätt i R2: med
     left:50% satt tjockleken mitt på kortet och läste som ett veck rakt genom
     en plan yta, inte som en kant. Ett kort är tjockt vid sin kant.
     transform-origin:100% 50% + rotateY(90deg) gör elementet till en 2 px rim
     som är gångjärnad i kortets högerkant och sträcker sig i djupled: kantställd
     och osynlig när kortet ligger platt, rakt mot betraktaren vid 90°.
     Opaciteten är parabeln upphöjd till tre, så rimmen tonar in sent och
     försvinner igen när kortet planar ut. Väg (d) 2 ur ASSETS.md § 3, och
     mattis-ribbans mätpunkt. */
  .plate-edge{position:absolute;right:0;top:0;bottom:0;width:2px;
    transform-origin:100% 50%;transform:rotateY(90deg);pointer-events:none;
